apply_ruleset:
Apply ruleset

Rules over records. Each rule says *if* some conditions hold *then* a record gets a category, such as a band, or a new value computed from its columns. The rules are written in the step's dialog, or read from a published ruleset.

What it does

It checks every rule against every record and gives each record what the rules concluded, as new columns. A record no rule matched keeps no conclusion, and the run says how many.

What you connect

Records: a table, points or polygons. Choose which under *Records arrive as*, in Configure…, then the step that feeds it under *Inputs*. A table imported wide, one row per subject and a column per variable, is read that way: one record per subject, its columns as the file named them. It gives back the same records with the new columns.

How to use it

Configure… opens the step's dialog. On a new step, choose a published ruleset, or *Write rules for this step*, and Apply: rules of your own open in the rules dialog. There, Records and columns comes first: how the records arrive, each column's kind and its unit. Then the settings, the rules, and the otherwise. Nothing changes until Apply.

Each part of a rule is a block, with its word and its colour, so a rule's shape reads at a glance:

BlockWhat it decides
if (blue)A column, a comparison (*is*, *is not*, *is more than*, *is at most*, *is less than*, *is at least*, *is recorded*, *is not recorded*) and a value: a typed number or one of the step's settings
+ andConditions in one *if* block, which must all hold
or (purple)An alternative *if* block, any of which will do
then (green), a categoryA new column and the value a matching record gets: *band* is *Short*
then, a computed valueA new column and a sum: *houses without a death* is *houses* minus *deaths*. Plus, minus, times or divided by; each side a column, a value another rule computed, or a typed number
otherwise (amber)A column's value for a record no rule gave one: *class* is *Cannot be classified*

Each block also has its own edge, solid, dotted, double or dashed, so the blocks are told apart without colour. The comparison in a condition is keyed by its family the same way: comparisons of numbers (*is more than*, *is at most*, *is less than*, *is at least*) teal; *is* and *is not* slate; *is recorded* and *is not recorded* rose, with a dotted edge.

A rule can read a category another rule gave. Once a rule concludes *lab* is *positive*, *lab* is offered as a column a condition can read, by that name. A category reads in the table as it was typed: *Cannot be classified*.

Is not matches a recorded value that differs: *rash is not No* matches *Yes* and *Unknown*. A value not recorded never matches *is not*; ask *is not recorded* for that.

Otherwise, one per column, gives the column a value where no rule did. It waits for the columns its rules read: a *class* read from *lab result* takes its otherwise only after *lab result* has had its own. So an ordered classification, such as WHO's for measles, is written as columns in stages, each a few rules and an otherwise. The rulesets worked example builds one, *Which suspected cases meet the case definition?* An otherwise never settles two rules that disagree: that record stays without a value, and is named.

+ Add a value computed for every record writes a rule with no condition: every record gets the value.

A new column states its unit, and what it measures, in the two boxes after the sum: *deaths per 10,000 houses*. The table the step gives out carries both. A new column without a unit is said in the dialog and the run.

Settings. *+ Add a setting* gives the step a number the rules compare against, such as a fever threshold of 38 degrees Celsius: a name, a value and a unit. A condition then reads *temperature_c is more than fever*, and the threshold can be changed without rewriting a rule.

Kinds. Each column is read as a number, a category, or true or false, offered from its values and changed under *Records and columns*. A file that stores counts as text, "34", offers them as a category: say they are a number, and the text is reported unreadable at the run, where Data quality can read it as numbers.

Units. Each column the rules read states its unit, under *Records and columns*. A setting compared with a column must be in the column's unit, and a sum or difference must be of two columns in the same unit; either is refused while the rule is written. Columns the rules do not read need no unit.

One rule can read what another computed. *deaths per house* is deaths divided by houses; *deaths per 10,000 houses* is deaths per house times 10,000. The order the rules are listed in does not matter.

A rule can read the previous row. *new cases* is *cumulative_cases* minus *cumulative_cases in the previous row*. Such a rule needs the records sorted, which is set above the rules:

SettingWhat it decides
Sort byThe column the rows are put in order by. Date columns are offered first. The file's own order is never used
Within eachThe columns that say whose rows these are, such as the place: each place's rows are sorted, and a row's previous one is its own place's
The previous row is*The row recorded before*, or *the day*, *the week* or *the month before*. Where that period has no row, the value is empty, and counted

The table comes out in this order. The preview is then Before, Sorted and After.

Before and after. The dialog's Preview shows the records as they arrive and as these rules would leave them, on every edit: each new column, and which rule each record matched. Each rule's heading says how many records it matched. The first 50 records are drawn; the counts are of all of them.

What it says instead of guessing

  • A division by zero gives an empty value, and is counted and named: *1 record has an empty value, from a division

by zero: Harbour.*

  • A value to compute from that is missing gives no value, and is named.
  • Two rules giving one record different values give it none, and both rules are named.
  • The first row of a place has no previous one. Its value is empty, counted and named.
  • Two rows for one period have no single previous row: both, and every later row of their place, get no value

rather than a guessed one, and are named.

  • A value that fell below the previous row's, such as a cumulative count corrected down, is kept as computed and

named.

  • A number without a unit stops the rules from running until its unit is stated, and a rule comparing two

different units is refused while it is being written.

  • A record that took an otherwise is counted by column, so a default is never read as a rule's conclusion: *2

records took class's otherwise, because no rule gave class a value.*

On a wide table, a computed value is a new variable of each subject: in the table it is one more row per subject, named for the new column, as Derive a value adds it.

A published ruleset opens in its own dialog: the ruleset, its settings, and as the preview what it decides, its basis and what it obliges. *Read them in the rule editor* shows its rules there, every control disabled. A newer version is under Decisions: the step stays on the version it was built on until you choose.

What it will not do

  • Order the rules. Every rule is checked against every record; an otherwise is a default, not a last rule.
  • Settle two rules that disagree. The record gets no value, and both rules are named.
  • Guess a unit, a kind or a column from its name.
  • Change a published ruleset in place. A copy can be edited on the step.

What this does not establish

That a rule is right for its question. Rules do exactly what they say, including what was meant and not written.
case_series:
Cases by period

An epidemic curve's counts. Cases per day, week or month, by a date whose kind you state: onset, report, death, specimen collection, or a date of unstated kind.

What it does

It counts the records in each period, or adds up a count each record carries, and keeps every period between the first and the last, empty ones as zero. A gap in a curve is a fact about the outbreak, so it is not closed up.

What you connect

Records arrive as decides the input:

  • points, one per record: a line list with a date, such as Hagelloch's 188 measles cases. Each record is one case,

or carries its count in Cases per record.

  • a table, each row a count: a table with a date key column, such as Snow's deaths by day or Brazil's notified

cases by municipality and week. Each row adds its value column to its period.

Changing it disconnects the input, because points and a table are not the same shape.

It gives back a table of periods and counts. ＋ Add epidemic curve draws it as a Chart.

How to use it

SettingWhat it decides
Event date attributeThe column holding the date, written as an ISO 8601 date (2024-01-07)
Which date is it?Onset, report, death, specimen collection, or other. It is written on the chart's axis and caption
PeriodDay; week, starting Monday (ISO 8601); week, starting Sunday (the epidemiological week); or month
Cases per recordPoints only, optional: a column holding how many cases each record stands for

Choose the week your data uses. Brazil's notification system and the United States count epidemiological weeks from Sunday, and Brazil's data_iniSE is that Sunday. Counted by the Monday week instead, each Sunday falls into the week of the Monday six days before it, and every bar is labelled a day early. A week is labelled by its first day: *Week beginning 2024-01-07*.

When the source does not say which date it is, choose *other*. The chart then says *a date of unstated kind*. Brazil's weekly counts are notified cases by epidemiological week, and the source does not say whether the week is of onset or of notification.

The chart's line under the title gives the total and what it was counted from: *423,795 cases from 4,692 records* when each record carries a count, *188 records* when each record is one case.

What it will not do

It will not guess a date. A value that is not an ISO 8601 date is left out and counted, never read as day-first or month-first.

It will not restrict the curve to a period. Use Select rows by value, a range of dates, before it.

It will not join places to dates. Snow's map has places and no dates, and his table has dates and no places.

What this does not establish

That the kind of date chosen is the one the counts were made by: that is the source's to say. And that a weekly count is complete: late notifications reach the last weeks after the data were taken.
chart_output:
Chart

An output widget. It draws bars: a set of labelled categories with a number each. It creates a named tab in Results and changes nothing about the data it is given.

What it does

It takes whatever you connect and draws a bar per category, or an estimate with its interval.

A table. One bar per row. The table already says which column names the categories and which number goes on the bar, so nothing is asked of you: a rate of deaths per 1,000 people across 32 sub-districts is 32 bars, labelled by sub-district, each as tall as its own rate. Any table works — a rate, a total within groups, a derived value, a related column, a two-by-two, a case series.

A reasoning result. One bar per category, counting records: by decision, by access zone, or by evidence tier. Categories with no records keep their bars, the order is the one the categories are defined in rather than alphabetical, and a value the application does not recognise is counted and shown separately instead of being folded into the others.

A summarised polygon layer. One bar per polygon, carrying the count of locations inside it or the total of a numeric field, whichever the summary holds.

Connect one of them. The chart draws what it is given, so there is no mode to set first and no question to answer before you have the shape.

What a bar's number is travels with the chart. A count of records is a count; a rate is a rate, printed as the number it is rather than rounded to a whole one, and the axis is titled with the unit the table declared — "per 1,000 people" — instead of "Recorded count".

A table's own chart is preferred where it has one. A rate carries a chart that knows things the rows alone cannot say: that the numerator and the denominator come from different vintages, and how many groups had too small a denominator to report. Those appear in the caption.

Rows with no value are drawn at zero and counted in the caption. A group whose rate was suppressed is not a group whose rate is zero, and a chart that quietly dropped it would be shorter than the table beside it.

How to use it

1. Add Chart and select it. 2. Pick what it should draw on one of the source lists — *Table*, *Reasoning result*, or *Polygon summaries*. Only the lists with something to offer are shown. 3. If the table keys on more than one column, choose which one labels the bars. With a single key column there is nothing to choose and nothing is asked. 4. Set the mark and the orientation. Bars read best horizontally when the labels are long or there are many of them; 32 sub-districts is many. 5. Name the Results tab, give the chart a title, a subtitle and axis titles if you want them in the figure, then run the workflow. 6. Optionally turn on the category legend, which colours each bar. It holds at most six categories, because the validated palette is six hues; past that, group the tail upstream rather than ask for a seventh colour.

Variables moving together through time: one panel each

When a table carries several variables in one column — what Table input's Wide shape makes of a file with a column per variable — set One panel per to that column. Each variable gets its own panel and its own scale, stacked on one shared axis, so a reader runs down one date and reads every series, and a lag shows as an offset between panels.

SettingWhat it decides
One panel perThe key column whose values become panels. *No panels* is one chart, as before
Mark for each panelBars or a line. *Automatic* is bars up to 60 points and a line beyond
Shade a period, From and ToDates shaded behind every panel, both days included. Offered when the axis is dates

A value missing from a panel is a gap in its line, never a zero. Panels draw up to 250,000 points, the same as a table holds; measured in Chromium, 100,000 points took about 10 seconds to draw and 250,000 about 30 (experiment 175). They are drawn by the Vega-Lite renderer; the plain renderer and the write-up figure say so instead of drawing them on one scale. Experiment 174.

Two y axes on one plot are not offered. The ratio between two axes is arbitrary, so it can make any two series look correlated. Aligned panels show timing, not effect: that visits rose with PM2.5 in the same week is not a measure of how much PM2.5 raises them.

An estimate with its interval: a lag-response or forest plot

A table that declares an interval, as every Regression table does, is drawn as a point at each estimate with a whisker from the lower to the upper limit. Choose the Category column the estimates are placed at. Keep one term upstream with Select rows by value; a table holding several terms gets one point per term, labelled with it.

For a ratio, a log scale and a dashed line at 1 are on by default. On a log scale a ratio and its inverse, 0.5 and 2, sit equally far from 1, and the line marks no association. The figure says both on its subtitle, with the interval's level. Log scale and A dashed line at 1 in the Inspector turn them off.

A category declared a number is placed as one. Append rows can declare its labels numbers in a unit, so lags of 0, 1, 2, 4 and 8 weeks sit at their distances and the axis is titled with the unit. Otherwise the categories are evenly spaced, in the table's order.

The Brazil dengue example's fourth workflow draws its five lag models this way: five Regression tables stacked by Append rows, the temperature term kept, one point per lag. Validation Lab check 36 rebuilds the stack and the points with pandas and agrees with every number. Experiment 181.

Each point is what the table holds, and no more. Five points from five separate models are not adjusted for each other, and a figure cannot add what the models left out.

It states its own shape in the write-up

Every run machines a note into Results on the Notes tab stating what this chart is made of. It carries the line the chart already states rather than writing over it, and adds the number of bars, the column they are one per, and a warning where a bar sits at zero — because a withheld value and a measured zero are drawn the same way.

The caption is yours. A caption states the subject, the population, the place and the period in your words, and none of that can be read off a chart. What this writes is what the chart declares about itself — the material you write the caption from, sitting beside it in the same section.

And it carries no number. A figure's number depends on where it sits in the write-up and on the venue you are preparing — set one figure aside and the ones after it move up — so the number is worked out when the document is rendered. Nothing here says "Figure 1".

Edit it and it forks into a note of your own, like any machined note; the machined one goes on being rewritten by every run.

Where it goes in the write-up

In the write-up, under, just below Results tab name in the Inspector, chooses the part of the Notes write-up this output's figure and its note go in: Introduction, Methods, Results or Discussion. Results is the default. A map of the study area belongs in the Introduction; a figure that shows how the analysis was done can go in Methods. References is not offered, because it holds works and not figures. The run's receipt states the section and whether you chose it, and a validation rule checks that the note describing the figure is filed in that same section.

What it will not do

It will not aggregate. One bar per row, per category or per polygon — it never adds rows together. If you want totals, total them upstream with Total within groups, where the arithmetic is visible and ends up in the receipt.

It will not choose a column for you. Where a table keys on several columns and you name none, it uses the first, and says which in the caption. Nothing is guessed from a column's name.

It will not merge two rows that share a category. They stay as two bars. Adding them would be a total nobody asked for, and rates cannot be added at all.

It will not draw more than 100 bars or estimates, and will not colour more than six categories.

It will not put a count and a concentration on one scale. Use panels.

It is not a time series by itself. Connect Cases by period and the periods come with it; a plain table of dates is a table, and its rows are drawn in the order they are in.

It does not filter, weight or reinterpret. Every record it is given is counted once, and the receipt records the renderer, its version, the specification and what each bar's number means.

Worked examples that use it

NYC child asthma and ozone, 2016 to 2025 draws daily visits, ozone, PM2.5 and temperature as four aligned panels for May to July 2023, with the June smoke days shaded.

Snow's South London water supply study, 1854 draws the 32 registration sub-districts as bars of deaths per 1,000 people, from the rate's own chart, so the figure carries the vintage caveat with it.
clip_points_to_area:
Keep points inside the area

A spatial operation. It takes a layer of points and a study area, and passes on the points that are in the area.

What it does

Every point is tested against the study area's outline, and the ones inside come out the other side. The ones outside are counted and reported, not passed on.

The test is the same one the coverage check and the map use. A point counted inside here is inside there, and a figure you quote from one agrees with the other.

Why you need it

A source gives you what its own request asked for, and almost every source is bounded by a rectangle: OpenStreetMap's query takes a bounding box, a cloud dataset is read by extent, a country export is clipped to one. A rectangle is not a jurisdiction. Draw North Kivu — long, curved, a province of the DRC — and its bounding box covers large parts of Uganda and Rwanda; a facility search inside it returned 961 places of which 526 stood in the neighbouring countries.

This widget is where that is decided, visibly, on the canvas. Before it existed the decision was made privately inside whichever widget happened to need it, which meant it could not be seen, changed, or recorded.

How to use it

1. Connect the study area to the area port and the point layer to the points port. Both are required: the question is about these points against that area. 2. Leave Keep points that sit exactly on the outline ticked unless you need strict containment. 3. Run. The step reports how many were inside, how many sat on the boundary and how many fell outside, and passes the kept points on to whatever you wire next.

If every point falls outside, the step refuses and says so with the counts — that usually means the area is not the one you meant, or the points are somewhere else entirely.

The one setting

Keep points that sit exactly on the outline. On by default. A point on the border is in that jurisdiction's edge, and silently folding it into one side or the other answers a question nobody asked. Turn it off for strict containment — which is what the OGC predicate sfWithin means, and it gives a different count on exactly the data where it matters.

Seeing what it set aside

Show the excluded points on a connected map. On by default. They are drawn in the colour the map already uses for points outside the area, and they are not passed to anything downstream — the next widget receives only what is in the area.

The count tells you how many were set aside. Seeing them tells you whether setting them aside was right: 526 facilities in a tight cluster over one border is a different fact from 526 scattered in every direction, and no number distinguishes those.

What it records

The receipt names the predicate the kept set answers to, whether boundary points were kept, and three counts: inside, on the boundary, outside. A reader can tell how many the source offered and how many this area accepted, which is the number a reviewer asks for.

What it will not do

It does not change a point. Nothing is moved, snapped or rounded; a point either is in the area or is not.

It does not know why a point is outside. A facility across a border, a coordinate entered the wrong way round and a geocoding error all look the same to a membership test. The coverage check is the widget for asking what to do about them, with reasons recorded.

It does not clip polygons or rasters. Those have their own widgets.

Worked examples that use it

None yet. It was built on 2026-10-20, from a defect found in a real study area.
deduplicate_points:
Deduplicate records

A comparison. It takes two or more point layers from different sources, finds the records that are the same place, and merges the pairs that agree. The pairs it is unsure about it gives to you.

What it does

Two sources over one study area draw the same hospital twice. A count of facilities is then wrong by however many of those there are, and no amount of care downstream fixes it, because nothing downstream knows which records were the same place.

This compares records across sources and asks two questions of every pair it considers:

  • Do the names agree? Either exactly, after normalising, or by similarity.
  • Are they in the same place? Within a distance you set.

Each question that answers yes is worth one point. A pair scoring two merges on its own. A pair scoring one waits for you, because the two questions disagree and that is a judgement rather than a calculation. A pair scoring none was never a candidate.

Rows of one table

Choose Rows of one table under The records are. The widget then takes one table and compares rows that share the columns identifying a row, by default the table's declared primary key. These are the rows Data quality reports as repeating a key.

PairWhat happens
Identical on every compared columnOne record entered twice: the later row is left out on its own
Any compared column differsWaits for you. Choose Two records, or Same record and which row to keep

The rows left out are named in the receipt, and the input table is not changed. A row is never dropped because it came second: keeping the first row of a pair that disagrees would silently delete a case.

What you connect

Two or more point layers, each from a different source. One layer has nothing to compare with, so two is the floor rather than the shape; use Add point input for a third and a fourth.

How to use it

The step's panel holds its Name, its Inputs, one sentence saying what it compares, and Configure…. After a run, Result says what it found: the pairs counted, the records merged away, and Review pairs where some wait for you. Under that, Manual, Evidence and Version, then Duplicate and Remove.

Configure… opens the step's dialog, where every setting is. The records are chooses *Points, in two or more sources* or *Rows of one table*; the settings below follow it. Nothing changes the workflow until Apply.

To match the names of one table to another's, such as a line list's districts to the boundaries', use Relate a column from another table and allow for spelling there.

SettingWhat it decides
Name attributeWhich attribute carries the name. name for most sources.
Name comparison*Exact* after normalising, or *Jaro–Winkler similarity*.
Similarity at or aboveThe similarity at which two names count as agreeing.
Compare pairs withinPairs further apart than this are never compared at all.
Count as the same place withinThe distance at which two records are in one place.
Merge automatically at a score ofTwo means both questions must agree.
Ask me at a score ofOne means a single agreement brings the pair to you.

Choosing the distances

These are the two numbers worth measuring rather than accepting. Sources digitise a facility differently — one marks the building, another the compound gate, a third the signpost on the road — so how far apart two records of one facility sit is a property of your sources. Run it once with a generous *compare pairs within*, read the distances on the pairs it offers you, and set *count as the same place within* from what you see.

Deciding a pair

Select the widget and choose Review pairs. The dialog shows one pair at a time, with:

  • Both records side by side, each under the name of the source it came from.
  • Every attribute either record carries, lined up in one table, with the fields that agree

marked apart from the fields that differ. This is usually what settles it: a second field agreeing, or a second field flatly disagreeing. A field missing on one side shows as a gap, because a missing value is not agreement.

  • How far apart the records are, how closely the names matched, and which of the two tests

agreed.

Answer The same place or Different places, and say why. The reason is required: a judgement nobody can read six months later is not a record of one. It is kept with the decision, and the decision is pinned to the records as they were — edit either record and the judgement lapses, rather than a stale answer riding on changed data. A decision can be taken back from the same dialog.

Reading what you get

A point layer with one record per place. A merged record keeps the first source's values and carries a mergedFrom attribute naming every record that went into it. Records with no usable location pass through untouched — they were never candidates, and nothing has been said about them.

The receipt records the whole rule: the name method and its threshold, both distances, both score thresholds, how many pairs were compared, how many the blocking rule withheld, how many matched, how many are still waiting, and for every candidate its score, its distance and its name similarity. A figure that reports a deduplicated count can therefore say what produced it.

What it will not do

  • It will not look inside one source. Comparison is across sources, so a layer's duplicates of

itself are not found.

  • It will not read abbreviations. HGR Goma and Hôpital Général de Référence de Goma are one

facility and this will not say so: there is no nickname dictionary, no transliteration, no phonetic key and no learned model. That pair reaches you in the review band, which is where the judgement belongs.

  • It will not merge on a name alone, at the settings it ships with. Two clinics in one town can

share a name; two unrelated facilities can stand twenty metres apart.

  • It will not decide for you. A pair in the review band stays two records until somebody

answers. The gate is on the merge, not on the run.

  • It cannot tell you the thresholds are right. They are declarations about your data, and the

only way to know is to look at the pairs it offers.

Where the method comes from

The contracts are those of EPIAI RECORDLINK — blocking before comparison, binary contributions rather than a blended score, three classes rather than merge-or-not, and a missing value that never agrees with another missing value. This widget adds the spatial comparison and the merge the thresholds licence.
derive_value:
Derive a value

Arithmetic. It takes a table, combines two of its values with one operation, and gives the table back with a new value added for every group of rows.

What it does

A table here is long: every row carries one value, under key columns. So two numbers about the same subject are two rows, not two columns. Snow's Table IX holds

suppliermeasurecount
Southwark and Vauxhall Companyhouses40,046
Southwark and Vauxhall Companydeaths1,263

and the number a 2×2 needs — houses without a death — is in neither row. It is houses minus deaths, and until this widget existed the only way to get it was to compute it somewhere else and import the answer.

This step computes it once per group: all the rows sharing the other key columns are one group, and measure is the column holding the names of the values to combine.

Seeing what this step did

After a run, View this table at the top of the Inspector opens the output. Before and After switch between the table that came in and the one that went out, and After says how many rows and columns there were before.

What you connect

records — a table. It gives back the same table with the derived rows added.

How to use it

SettingWhat it decides
Key column holding the valuesWhich column names the values. In Snow's table, measure.
First valueThe left operand, e.g. houses.
Operationminus, plus, times, divided by.
Second valueThe right operand, e.g. deaths.
Name for the derived valueWhat the new rows are called, e.g. houses without a death.

The values are offered as a list wherever the chain ends in a table this canvas holds, including through an earlier *Derive a value* or *Select rows by value*. Where it does not, you type them.

What it refuses, and why

A group missing either value gets no row, and is named in the evidence. A supplier whose house count nobody recorded has an *unknown* number of houses without a death. Writing a zero there would be a measurement the table never made.

A name the column already uses is refused. Two rows would then share a key, and a table with two values for one key is one nobody can read.

Dividing by zero is unknown, not infinite.

What it will not do

It will not tell you whether the two values can be combined. Subtracting deaths from houses works because both count houses; subtracting a rate from a count is equally allowed here and is nonsense. Check that yourself before reading the answer.

It will not fill in a group whose values are incomplete. Those groups come back named, with no derived row, and any figure you draw from the result is missing them — count them before you present it.

It will not reach across tables. Both values must already be in the one table you connect.

What this does not establish

The widget does not know what its numbers count. Subtracting deaths from houses is sound only because both count houses; subtracting a rate from a count is equally permitted here and is nonsense. Nothing checks that the two values are commensurable, because nothing in the table says so — the unit belongs to the table as a whole, not to each measure.

A derived value is also not a measurement. houses without a death was never observed; it is an inference from two things that were, and it inherits every error in both.
find_health_facilities:
Find health facilities

A source of facility points, two ways: every facility a source records inside a study area, or the facility each row of a list names.

What it does

Inside a study area, it fetches the health facilities a source records there. From a list, it finds the facility each row names in a national register, and marks how sure the match is. Either way it hands on points, each carrying where it came from.

How to use it

Add it from the library, then choose the way in under Configure…: *Inside the study area* or *From a list*. Each is described below.

Inside the study area

Connect a Study area: it is the scope of the query. In Configure…, choose the source (OpenStreetMap live, the Humanitarian OpenStreetMap Team's country export, or Overture Maps Places), the kinds of facility, and whether to keep only named ones; each source's licence is shown before anything is fetched. Then Retrieve facilities. The Result says how many were kept and how many were dropped, and why.

From a list

For a list that names facilities, such as a line list's organisation units. In Configure…, choose *From a list*, then:

SettingWhat it decides
Column naming the facilityThe list's column holding each row's facility name
Column naming its areaOptional: a district or similar, to tell apart two facilities of one name
Registers, matched in this orderFacility lists from the registers declared in the ontology: GRID3 for Sierra Leone, Nigeria and DR Congo, and OpenStreetMap for any country. A name is looked for in the first register, then the next. A register that cannot be read is shown and cannot be chosen
Country to read OpenStreetMap forShown when OpenStreetMap is chosen. It starts as the other registers' country

Then Fetch the registers: a register is fetched once and kept on this device.

OpenStreetMap is matched by name only. It has no facility types, so a name it matches allowing for spelling is held for your review under Decisions. It has no point until you choose. A name it matches exactly is handed on. Put it after a national register, for what that register does not have. Its points are under the Open Database License, which is share-alike: anything made from them is under it too.

Every row gets one outcome, and none is dropped:

OutcomeWhat it means

matched allowing for spellingOne facility's name within the tolerance, the same type. From OpenStreetMap, held for your review
type differsThe name matches and the type does not, as MCHP against CHP: for your review
ambiguousSeveral facilities could be the one named: choose, under Decisions
an area, not a facilityNo point, said

The dialog's Preview counts them, by name and by row, before you apply. Decisions lists each ambiguous name, each type that differs and each spelling held, with its candidates, so you choose the facility it means, or none. Rows with a facility become points carrying the outcome, the register's name and identifier, and the score.

What it will not do

  • Place anyone at home. A point is where the register places the facility.
  • Guess. A type that differs, an ambiguous name, a spelling held, an area and a name not found have no point until you decide.
  • Geocode an address or a place that is not a facility.

What this does not establish

That a source records every facility that exists: an absence is not evidence of absence. That 0.88 suits every country's names: it was checked by hand on Sierra Leone's. That OpenStreetMap's spellings can be trusted anywhere: on Sierra Leone's names, 4 of 7 that could be checked against GRID3 were the wrong facility.
group_table:
Total within groups

Addition, or a count. It takes a table, keeps the key columns you name, and adds up the values of every row that agrees on them, or counts those rows.

What it does

32 sub-districts, each with a population and a death count, each belonging to one of three water supply categories. Totalling within the supply category and the measure turns 64 rows into six: the people and the deaths in each category. That six-row table is a contingency table, and it is what the next steps turn into a two-by-two.

Shares within groups

Tick Add each group's share, % and every group gets its share beside its count or total. Under Share within, tick the columns whose groups each make 100%: a line list counted by classification and by what was recorded, with the share within classification, shows how a classification's cases divide. Tick none and each share is of the whole table.

The result has a column statistic naming each number, the count and the share, and the table view shows them side by side. A share is held to one decimal place, so a classification can total 99.9 or 100.1. A share is offered with Sum and Count rows, which add up to a total, and not with a minimum or a maximum. A share of a total that is unknown, because a group summed over an empty cell, is unknown too.

Seeing what this step did

After a run, View this table at the top of the Inspector opens the output. Before and After switch between the table that came in and the one that went out, and After says how many rows and columns there were before.

What you connect

records — any table.

How to use it

Connect a table, then open Configure…. The Preview shows the table your settings make, and nothing changes until Apply.

SettingWhat it decides
Key columns to keepThe key columns that survive. Rows agreeing on all of them become one row.
AggregateSum, Minimum, Maximum or Count rows
Total what is present, excluding empty cellsOff: a group holding an empty cell totals to nothing known. On: what was recorded is totalled, and the receipt and the write-up say so
Add each group's share, %A share beside each count or total
Share withinThe columns whose groups each make 100%. None ticked: the whole table

Why you name what is kept rather than what is dropped

Because files change. Name the columns you keep and a column added to the file later is simply dropped, leaving you the same groups you had before. Name the columns you drop and that new column silently becomes a grouping key, splitting your groups without telling you.

Counting a line list

A line list has no count in it: Oswego's 75 people are a row each, with a Y or an N under every food. Choose Count rows and each group holds how many rows agree, which is what a two-by-two needs. Keep the exposure and the outcome and the four cells come out.

Count rows never reads the value, so a blank is still a row and the result's value is called rows. It counts rows, not people. Import one value column from a line list: two value columns give two rows per person, and each person then counts twice. The step cannot detect that.

Why it only adds up

Adding counts gives you a count. Adding rates gives you a number with no referent — deaths per 1,000 in three sub-districts do not add up to deaths per 3,000 in one. This step cannot tell a count from a rate, so it offers the operation that is right for counts and does not offer a choice it has no way to police. Averages are a different operation and are not built.

Reading what you get

One row per group, and a receipt stating which columns were kept, which were dropped, how many rows collapsed into how many groups, and every group that held an empty cell.

What it will not do

  • It will not treat an empty cell as a zero. A group holding any empty value totals to

nothing known, and is named in the receipt. This is the whole risk of the operation: summing over an empty cell gives a total that is too small by an amount nobody can state, and a stratum whose population was never recorded should come out *unknown* rather than *small*.

  • It will not check that the rows belong together. You named the columns; it adds up what

agrees on them. If you ask it to total a column of rates it will do that, and the number will mean nothing.

  • It will not group by everything. That is a no-op, and it says so rather than handing back

your table unchanged.

Where it is used

The South London example: *Died or survived, by water supply*.

What this does not establish

That a share is the measure you need. A share of rows is not a rate: it has no denominator of people unless each row is one person.

How it was checked

Validation Lab check 29, 29-group-table-vs-pandas.ipynb, against a pandas groupby. All six totals of the Snow contingency table agree exactly — they are integer counts, so the tolerance is zero rather than small.

The empty cell is the case worth checking, and pandas has no option for the rule this widget states. min_count=1 reads like it and is the first thing anyone writes: it bounds how many values must be *present*, not whether any are *absent*, so on eleven numbers and one empty cell it returns the eleven. On this data that is 147,945 people instead of nothing known — short by the one sub-district nobody recorded. The comparison that does hold is a per-group sum(skipna=False).

Validation Lab check 39, 39-group-shares-vs-pandas.ipynb, recomputes the shares with pandas on the same table: each company's share of the people and of the deaths, a count's share of all, and one emptied cell. Every number agrees exactly, in CPython and in the browser kernel.

What no check can verify is the protection that matters most here: summing is the only operation offered, because this step cannot tell a count from a rate.
isochrone:
Network isochrone

A process widget. It draws the area you can reach on foot within a stated time, walking along real streets, from one or more sites.

What it does

From each site it walks outward along the street network until the time runs out, then draws a band around every street it reached. The result is one region per site — not a circle, because streets are not straight and do not go everywhere.

A walk has three parts and this charges for all three: to the nearest junction, along the streets, and off the street at the end to reach a door.

What you connect

ConnectWhat it needs
your sitesthe points to walk from — pumps, clinics, depots
a street networkfrom the Street network widget

Out come polygons, one per site. Draw them on a Map, or count your records into them with Summarize points in polygons.

How to use it

1. Add it from the palette, under Catchments. 2. Connect your sites and a street network. 3. Set the budget. *Minutes* × *metres per minute* is how far someone can walk — 5 minutes at 75 m/min is 375 m of street. 4. Set the final walk off the street — how far from a street someone can get to a door. The band is this wide where there is time left and narrower where there is not. 5. Set the snap limit — how far a site may be from the nearest street before the result says so. 6. Check the zone. Measuring happens in metres, so the UTM zone is part of the answer, and every measuring step in one workflow must agree on it. The run is refused by name if they disagree. 7. Run the workflow, then read the regions on a map and the alert in the Inspector.

How the travel time is spent

Shortest paths are Dijkstra over the network's directed edges and the metre lengths it supplies, including the partial length of a curved edge where the budget runs out part-way along it.

All three legs of the journey are charged against the same budget:

LegWhat it costs
the straight walk from the site onto the networkdistance to the snapped street, at walking speed
the streetsthe shortest path, by directed edge and supplied length
the final walk off the street to a doorthe band width where time allows it, narrower where it does not

Charging the last leg rather than adding it is what stops a region overshooting the time it is drawn for. The off-street band is an approximation of coverage beside the streets, and holes inside it remain unless infill is enabled.

Two cases are marked rather than dropped, and the widget names both:

  • A site further from a street than the snap limit is routed anyway and marked off-network.
  • A site whose walk onto the network alone spends the budget gets no catchment at all.

Coverage can also be cut short by the graph itself: a region stops where the downloaded network stops, which is a property of the extent that was downloaded and not of the travel time.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat it does there
John Snow · walking catchmentsfive-minute walking regions around the eight Soho pumps, drawn as a plot and as an interactive map, with the 1854 deaths counted into them

What it will not do

  • It is not a service area or a routed travel time. It is an approximation of shape, drawn

to be read. Nobody agreed to it and no router produced it.

  • It assumes the ground beside a street can be walked, at walking speed, in any direction.

Near the edge of the budget that is where the region is most generous.

  • It does not drop a site that is far from the streets. Such a site is routed anyway, with

the straight line to the nearest junction charged against its budget. Its region is marked, the widget glows red, and the Inspector names the leg. That straight line assumes you can cross whatever lies between, so the region reaches further than the ground allows.

  • A site whose walk to the street would spend the whole budget gets no region at all. It

reaches nothing in the stated time, which is the answer. It is named in the alert, and the note on the result says the counts are over the sites that reached something.

The direction it misleads

All of the above push the same way: a poorly connected place looks better served than it is. Streets and footpaths are mapped unevenly, and informal settlements least of all. Read a region over sparsely mapped ground as optimistic, check the alert for sites routed off the network, and check how far each site had to go to reach a street.

Checking it yourself

The lab's snapping notebook measures the displacement on the example data, and the corridor check rebuilds the region from the stated rule with Shapely.
join_table_to_area:
Join a table to the study area

A join. It takes a table of values and a study area whose parts are named, matches each row to the part it names, and hands on polygons that carry the value. A map downstream can then shade them.

What it does

A rate per sub-district and a boundary of sub-districts are two separate things until something puts one onto the other. Without that, the only map you can draw from a table of measures is a map of where the rows are, which for most data is a map of where people live.

What is being joined is a table and another table with geometry. A GeoJSON feature, a shapefile row and a GeoDataFrame row are each a row with a geometry column, so a boundary file carries attributes exactly as a CSV does. This widget matches the two on one named column.

What you connect

  • records — a table. Any widget that emits one will do: an imported table, a rate, a case

series. The column you match on must be one of its key columns.

  • area — a study area whose parts carry names. An area drawn by hand has no named parts, so

there is nothing to key on and this says so rather than drawing an empty choropleth that looks like a finding.

Or a polygon layer. Connect a *Polygon layer* in place of a study area when there are many parts. A study area is one extent of about 26,000 vertices, and Nigeria's 774 LGAs are about 218,000. The layer's name property is what rows are matched on. Connect one or the other.

Joining twice adds a column: what a polygon holds is kept. Join coverage and then zero-dose counts and each LGA carries both, which is what a rule needs to read both. A layer joined this way can be matched on a code, which matters where names repeat: 5 of Nigeria's LGA names belong to two places each.

How to use it

SettingWhat it decides
Column naming each partWhich of the table's key columns holds the part name. Offered from the connected table, not typed.
Match names*Ignoring punctuation and spacing*, or *Exactly as written*.

Choosing how names are matched

Names are compared for equality, never for resemblance. There is no similarity score and no threshold to set, because a name either is the name of that part or it is not.

Ignoring punctuation and spacing is what matches St. George, Camberwell to St. George Camberwell. On Snow's South London files it is the difference between 23 of 32 rows matching and 32 of 32: the nine that fail differ only by a comma. It will not match an abbreviation to a full name, or a historical spelling to a modern one, and it says so rather than guessing.

If your files differ by more than punctuation, this widget is the wrong tool and will tell you which rows it could not place. Fix the names at the source, where the correction is a fact about the data rather than a setting on a node.

Reading what you get

Polygons, one feature per part, each carrying the matched row's value and the rest of its columns. The parts are kept separate rather than dissolved.

  • A part no row names is drawn and left empty, in a neutral shade — never in the lowest class.

An unmatched boundary drawn pale reads as a finding of low incidence, which is the opposite of what it means.

  • Two parts sharing a name both take the value. That is true of a rate and is not true of a

count: Streatham is two polygons, and both carry its rate, which is why Snow's 32 sub-districts draw as 33 parts.

  • The parts of one unit are not two places. A municipality of several islands is one unit of several parts:

each part takes the value, and none of this is reported as a repeated name. Rio de Janeiro state's 92 municipalities draw as 155 parts.

The receipt records the column matched on, the normalisation used, how many rows matched, how many did not, and every part left without a value, so a figure made from this can say what produced it.

What it will not do

  • It will not guess at a name. No similarity, no threshold, no review band. A row it cannot

place is reported, not approximated.

  • It will not aggregate. Two rows naming the same part are a duplicate-key problem in the

table, and are reported as one rather than quietly summed or averaged.

  • It will not decide whether the number is worth mapping. Whether the rate was computed over

the right denominator, whether the classes are honest, and whether a reader will take area for magnitude are questions this widget does not answer.

How it was checked

Validation Lab check 31, 31-area-join-vs-pandas.ipynb, against a pandas left merge. Every part takes the value a merge gives it, nulls included, and the counts agree — 33 of 33 parts and 32 of 32 rows after folding, with Streatham's two parts carrying one value between them.

What the folding bought, measured. On the raw strings only 23 of 32 rows match. The nine that need folding are all a comma: the table writes St. George, Camberwell where the boundary file writes St. George Camberwell. A join on raw keys would have drawn a choropleth missing 28% of its sub-districts. The check also confirms the folding touched nothing *but* punctuation — it is not reimplemented there, because a second copy by the same author is not a second opinion, so what is checked is the property it must satisfy.

And the data cannot supply a negative control, which is worth knowing when you rely on this. Snow's table and these boundaries contain no pair differing by more than punctuation, so nothing in the example tests a name that *ought* not to match — 32 of 32 is also what a rule that matched too readily would score. The check constructs one: a part renamed to Camberwell Green, which this join reports unmatched. Jaro-Winkler to Camberwell is 0.925, so a similarity-based linkage at the usual 0.90 threshold would have accepted it. That figure is what having no threshold here is worth.

Frames

Frames from names a key column whose values are frames, such as measure holding dtp1_2005 to dtp1_2024. Each part then carries one value per frame, and an interactive map can play through them. The part's single value is the last frame's. A key repeated across frames is expected; a key repeated within a frame is reported.
map_image_input:
Georeferenced map image

What it does

Draws a scanned or published map underneath your workflow, in your workflow's own projection, so a modern result sits over historical ground.

It was built for John Snow's 1855 Map 2, whose blue, red and purple washes show which company supplied which part of south London — and whose purple intermingled zone is the whole point of his design. Put the sub-district boundaries over it and a reader can see for themselves whether the two agree.

What you connect

Nothing goes in. It is a source: you give it an image and a georeference.

Its output goes to a Map, on the ground port.

How to use it

1. Add it and choose the image — a JPEG or PNG of a map. 2. Give it the georeference, either as a world file (.jgw, .pgw, .wld) or as four corners in degrees: west, south, east, north. 3. Connect it to a Map, and set the opacity so you can read what is drawn on top.

Reading what you get

The figure says which plate it drew, where it came from, and about how many metres one of its pixels covers. Snow's plate over south London is about 16 metres per pixel: enough to recognise the river and the parish outlines, not enough to read a street.

The receipt records the image's digest, its pixel size, the four bounds, that ground resolution, and layerRole "context".

What it will not do

  • It will not let you measure it. The output carries its own port type, so it cannot be

connected to Clip raster or Sample raster at all. A plate's pixels are a printer's ink: sampling them returns the colour of a line, which is a number with no referent. This is the one thing the widget refuses by construction rather than by warning.

  • It will not join anything to what the map shows. A boundary drawn on an 1855 plate is a

picture of a boundary. Use a study area for the frame.

  • It will not draw a rotated plate. If the world file carries rotation terms, it stops and says

so. Drawing a rotated image as an upright rectangle would put the map in the wrong place while looking entirely correct.

  • It will not reproject. The corners are read as CRS84 degrees. Corners outside the world

usually mean a projected georeference, and it refuses rather than reading one datum's coordinates as another's — an error that moves a map by hundreds of metres and still looks like a map.

  • It will not tell you the georeference is right. It draws where you said. An alignment error

looks exactly like a correct placement.

Where it is used

The South London example: Snow's Map 2 under the sub-district choropleth.

How it was checked

Unit tests over the world-file reader, the bounds it derives from it, the ground resolution, and each refusal — a rotated world file, a flipped image, crossed corners and corners outside the world. A browser test places a plate under a figure and confirms it is drawn beneath the workflow's own layers rather than over them.

What no test establishes is whether the georeference is correct. See [experiment 143](../experiments/143-a-georeferenced-plate-as-ground.md), which records that measuring the residual at the plate's four control points against modern boundaries is what would close it, and that it has not been done.
map_output:
Map

An output widget. It draws what your workflow produced. It computes nothing, changes nothing and decides nothing — if a number looks wrong on the map, the step that produced it is where to look.

What it does

A map is a stack of layers, drawn in order from the ground up:

1. a basemap, if you choose one — streets or terrain, under everything else 2. a study area, as the ground your results sit on 3. polygons — catchments, hulls, cells or bands 4. points — your records, sites, or anything with a location 5. a raster or a street network, where you have one

You connect what you want drawn. There is no setting that says what kind of map this is.

What you connect

ConnectTo draw
a study areathe boundary your work is inside
a point layerrecords with locations — up to eight separate layers
catchment polygonsareas reached, covered or grouped
a reasoning resultpoints coloured by the decision a ruleset reached
a coverage checkpoints marked inside, outside or missing a location
a rasterprepared or clipped cells
a street networkthe streets themselves

How to use it

1. Add the Map from the palette, under Outputs. 2. Connect your first layer. Drag from any step that produced something drawable onto the map's + Add a layer port, or pick it from Add a layer under *Inputs* in the Inspector. The map works out which port it belongs to. 3. Add more layers the same way. A second point source gets a layer of its own rather than replacing the first. 4. Open Configure… for everything about how it is drawn. Nothing changes until Apply, and Apply redraws the map without running the workflow again. 5. Choose how it is drawn. *Static plot* exports as an SVG with a scale bar and a north arrow. *Interactive map* can be panned and zoomed, and is the only one that can show a basemap. 6. Choose a basemap if the geography matters — streets or terrain under your results. Leaving it at *None* keeps the map working with no connection at all. 7. Title it, and write the source note. Both appear on the map and in its export. 8. Run the workflow. The map appears as a Results tab. Manage layers… orders, names and groups the layers it draws.

Reading what you get

  • The key names every layer drawn.
  • The scale bar and north arrow appear on a static plot. An interactive map has no

single scale, so it shows neither.

  • The source note carries whatever you wrote, plus the licence of anything the map used.

Symbols and colour

Two things about a point are shown at once, in two separate channels, so neither has to be read off the other.

  • Colour says which layer the point came from. Each point layer you connect gets its own hue

from the categorical palette, so two searches of two different sources are told apart on the map and listed separately in the layer control, where either can be switched off.

  • Fill says where the point stands. Filled inside the study area, hollow outside it, grey when

the record has no usable location — those are not drawn on the map and are listed instead.

  • Each layer also gets a mark: circle, square, triangle, star, cross or X. A mark is chosen per

layer in this widget's settings, and the legend draws the same mark the map draws. Colour alone is not readable by every reader, and a figure printed in greyscale has no colour at all.

  • Every symbol carries a dark outline, so it reads over any basemap — a terrain basemap runs

through the same colours the palette uses, and a hollow mark over one is hard to pick out. It is a neutral, not a seventh colour, and a checkbox turns it off for a pale ground or a printed figure.

  • Ordered values use an ordered ramp. Travel-time bands run light to dark through one hue,

which is a ColorBrewer sequential scheme. A category palette on an ordered variable invites the reader to see difference where there is sequence.

The map's receipt records all of this — which channel carries which variable, the palette and the authority it comes from, and each layer's mark and colour with whether you chose it or the map derived it — so a figure in a publication can be attributed.

Where it goes in the write-up

In the write-up, under, in Configure…, chooses the part of the Notes write-up this output's figure and its note go in: Introduction, Methods, Results or Discussion. Results is the default. A map of the study area belongs in the Introduction; a figure that shows how the analysis was done can go in Methods. References is not offered, because it holds works and not figures. The run's receipt states the section and whether you chose it, and a validation rule checks that the note describing the figure is filed in that same section.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat the map shows
John Snow · outbreak extentthe judged outline over 250 death locations
John Snow · Voronoi catchmentsone catchment per pump, with deaths overlaid
John Snow · walking catchmentstravel-time bands, as a plot and as an interactive map
Old Naledi · diagnostic accessfacilities coloured by the decision a ruleset reached
Old Naledi · raster clippinga clipped raster inside its boundary
Sea-level rise at Manila’s health facilities (its own repository)the study area, 194 facilities and the eight AR6 tide gauges
Geoprivacythe same records before and after being moved

It states its own shape in the write-up

Every run machines a note into Results on the Notes tab stating what this map is made of. The layers bottom to top, their feature counts, and any layer that is connected and not drawn — which is a fact about the figure a reader is owed. It is read off the same layer list the figure and the key draw from, so it cannot disagree with the picture.

The caption is yours. A caption states the subject, the population, the place and the period in your words, and none of that can be read off a map. What this writes is what the map declares about itself — the material you write the caption from, sitting beside it in the same section.

And it carries no number. A figure's number depends on where it sits in the write-up and on the venue you are preparing — set one figure aside and the ones after it move up — so the number is worked out when the document is rendered. Nothing here says "Figure 1".

Edit it and it forks into a note of your own, like any machined note; the machined one goes on being rewritten by every run.

What it will not do

  • It cannot draw everything at once. A map with both a raster and polygons connected draws

the raster. The layers stay connected; only one is drawn. A street network is no longer one of these cases: points, a study area and a street network wired to one map are all drawn together, on the interactive presentation.

  • The static plot does not draw a street network beside points. The streets are drawn in a

frame of their own size, so a map carrying both draws the points in the plot and says where the streets are. Set the presentation to interactive to see all of it in one picture.

  • It cannot reorder layers, or choose their colours. Draw order is fixed, and a layer's hue

comes from its position in the palette. The mark is the one part of the symbol you choose.

  • A basemap is not included in the SVG export. The tiles come from an outside service as

you look at the map, so a figure you export shows your layers on a blank ground.

  • Choosing a basemap sends the area you are viewing to that service. Everything else about

this map works offline. For maps of sensitive locations that is worth knowing before you switch it on.

  • It cannot tell you whether a map is honest. Emphasis, framing and colour all change how a

map reads, and none of them changes a number. See the layers you connected, and say in the source note what the map is about.
measure_distance:
Measure distance

For each point, the nearest of a set of candidates, and how far it is. Each facility's nearest tide gauge; each sampled location's nearest clinic.

What it does

It measures the straight-line distance from every point to every candidate and keeps the nearest, on a sphere of 6,371.0088 km (Haversine). It gives one row per point: the point, its nearest candidate, and the distance.

What you connect

  • Points to measure from: any point layer.
  • Candidates, the nearest of which is found: any point layer.

A step that reads a table, such as Relate, Select rows or Table, reads the result as a table with these columns:

ColumnHolds
point_idThe point
nearest_idIts nearest candidate
nearest_<attribute>Each of that candidate's own attributes: nearest_name, nearest_site_id
distanceThe distance, in the unit chosen

So Relate can bring a value that belongs to the candidate onto each point: the sea-level example matches nearest_site_id to the projections' site_id.

How to use it

The step's panel holds its Name, its two inputs, one sentence saying what it measures, and Configure…:

SettingWhat it decides
Distances inkilometres or metres
Eligible candidatesConditions on a candidate's own attribute: its value is, or is not, one of those you list. A candidate without the attribute does not match

What it will not do

  • It will not follow roads or water. A straight-line distance is not a travel distance.
  • It will not say a point belongs to its nearest candidate. Nearest is a fact about distance; what it means is yours

to state.

  • A point with no location keeps its row, with no nearest candidate and no distance, so it is counted.

Where it is used

The Old Naledi example (sampled locations and the nearest eligible clinic) and the sea-level example (each facility's nearest tide gauge).
network_input:
Street network

An input widget. It supplies the streets that walking-distance work is measured along: a graph of points joined by segments, each with a length.

Three ways in

Choosing one shows that method's controls and hides the others, so the panel describes the path you are on.

Upload a network file. A GraphML or JSON graph prepared elsewhere. It keeps its own extent.

Download from OpenStreetMap. The study area's bounds go to overpass-api.de, which is asked to count what it would send before anything is sent, so an area past the limit is refused rather than transferred and discarded. One request at a time, 60 seconds minimum between them plus 30 seconds per megabyte received: the service is donated and the pause is the courtesy.

Read an extract on this device. A published .osm.pbf — Geofabrik's country files, or any other OSM extract — chosen with the file picker. The file is read where it sits and is never copied into this browser's storage; the study area's bounding box is applied while the extract is decoded, so a country file yields one province's streets. Most countries have no province-level extract published, which is the point: the same file serves every province and every workflow after the first, and nothing is downloaded twice.

The travel mode belongs to all three. Walking keeps footways, paths and steps; driving keeps roads and honours vehicle one-ways. At the scale of a province the choice decides how much there is to read; at the scale of a district it decides what the question means. An acquired ADM1 or ADM0 study area defaults to driving, because nobody walks across a province.

What it does

It gives the workflow a walkable street network, either downloaded from OpenStreetMap for your study area or uploaded from a file you prepared elsewhere.

A downloaded network keeps the ways people can walk on — residential streets, footways, paths, steps, tracks, service roads and the ordinary road classes — and leaves out anything tagged as closed to pedestrians. Each way becomes a run of segments between the points it was drawn with.

Graph limit. The limit counts every point in the graph, including each bend a street was drawn with, not only the places two streets meet. A town can hold three points for every real intersection and a road following a coastline can hold seventeen, so the same limit allows very different amounts of street in different places. The download size allowed follows this number, so raising it raises what can be fetched.

What you connect

It takes an area — the study area that says where to download — and emits a network, which the isochrone, the junction reachability step, the corridor and the snapping step all accept. A map can draw one directly.

How to use it

1. Connect a Study area, then open the Street network node. 2. Leave Input method on *Download from OpenStreetMap*, or switch to upload if you have a file. 3. Press Check endpoint status if you want to know what the servers can do right now: it reports free slots and, when there are none, when the next one frees. 4. Press Download and save OSM network. This is a separate action — running the workflow does not start a download. 5. If the area is large or the streets dense, raise the graph limit and download again.

Downloads are paced: one at a time, with a pause afterwards that grows with the size of what you received. A busy server is waited for rather than treated as a failure. A network you have already downloaded is kept, so asking the same question again costs no request at all.

What it will not do

It does not download while you run the workflow. Acquisition is always something you ask for.

An area too large for one request is asked for in several, automatically. The single request is tried first; if the service's own count says it will not fit, the panel says so — *"Too much for one request — working out how many parts it takes"* — and then works through the tiles, reporting each. The grid comes from that count, so a dense city is divided more finely than an empty district of the same size, and a sparse area is still one request. Tiles overlap by the download margin so a street crossing a seam keeps both ends, and parts of the grid that miss your study area are never requested at all. Stop ends the whole sequence, and the pause earned is charged once for the total rather than once per part.

Whatever route it took, the result is clipped to your study area polygon, not to the box around it. A junction outside the outline is not in the network unless it falls within your download margin, which is fetched on purpose so journeys near the border still work; a road is cut at the border rather than trailing beyond it. The widget records how many junctions and segments that removed.

It does not stop a download that is arriving. A request that never begins to answer is given three minutes, which is a limit on waiting, not on downloading. Once the first bytes arrive there is a download in progress and no clock ends it, however long it takes: press Stop when you want to give up, and the panel says how much had arrived and that none of it was kept. While it runs the panel shows how much has arrived and how fast, averaged over the last few seconds, so a transfer in trouble reads as a falling number rather than a frozen one. If it goes quiet for ninety seconds the panel says that too, with how much had arrived, and keeps waiting for you to decide.

It does not offer to hand-edit a large graph. The Edit bounded network JSON box is for the kind of network a person writes or fixes by hand — the Soho graph is about 28 KB. Above 20,000 nodes-plus-edges it is not offered, and the panel says so. Serialising a province into that box cost 41.8 MB of pretty-printed JSON and 59.7 MB again after escaping, rebuilt every time the panel redrew, which was enough to kill the browser tab while nothing was being done. The file input beside it stays, so a large graph can still be replaced by a small one, and nothing about the graph itself changes: it is held, drawn, run and exported at any size. The limit is declared as the cap json-editor-elements, queryable in the ontology like the rest.

It does not guess your area. Without a connected study area there is nothing to bound the request.

It downloads one travel mode at a time. Choose walking or driving before you download, because the two are different graphs and not two labels on one:

Walking keepsDriving keeps
Footways, paths, steps, pedestrian waysyesno
Motorways, trunk roads and their slip roadsnoyes
Ordinary streets — residential, unclassified, tertiary to primaryyesyes
One-way restrictions it obeysthe ones that apply on footvehicle one-ways, and roundabouts

A saved graph keeps the mode it was downloaded for, and the widget says which. To change mode, change it here and download again: the new graph replaces the old one. A widget further down the workflow that asks for a mode this graph cannot carry refuses the run and says so, rather than reporting minutes for a journey the streets do not support.

Distances along it are distances on those streets, and a network downloaded today describes the streets today, not the streets of whatever period your data comes from.

Before anything large is downloaded, the widget asks the service how much is there. Overpass answers that question directly, and an area holding more street data than this widget can take is refused with the number — after one cheap request rather than after several large ones that fail. An area so large that the service will not even count it is refused the same way, because that is what a public instance says when an area is beyond what it will process.

A saved network is kept beside the workflow rather than inside it, in the larger store your browser offers, so the size of a graph is no longer limited by what a workflow may hold. If that store is unavailable — private browsing, for instance — the application says "small store only" when it saves, and a large network may then be refused.

A driving graph carries no speed limits, no junction delay and no congestion. Travel time over it is one speed applied to every street, which is the same model walking uses and a weaker one for a car.

Worked examples that use it

John Snow network isochrones, in the 1854 Cholera Outbreak in London project, uses a prepared Soho network to draw what each pump could be reached from on foot.
point_input:
Point data

An input widget. It brings located records into a workflow — one row per thing, each with a position and whatever attributes came with it.

What it does

It holds a set of points and the values attached to them: cases, households, facilities, pumps, sample sites. Everything downstream that works on points starts here.

Records arrive three ways. Import a file — GeoJSON, or a CSV with longitude and latitude columns. Place pins by clicking a map, for a handful of locations you know. Connect a source that produces points, such as a facility search.

A record may have no position. That is kept rather than dropped, because a case with no recorded address is still a case, and steps that need geometry say how many they had to leave out instead of quietly working with fewer.

Columns and their kinds. Each attribute has a declared kind — number, text, or a term from a list you give. The data quality panel profiles a column, shows which values do not match its kind, and offers a repair. A repair is recorded with the node and appears in the run evidence; it never overwrites what the file held.

What you connect

It has no input unless you connect a source. Its output is points, which nearly everything accepts: maps, tables, distance measurement, catchments, summaries, rates, case series and the geoprivacy steps.

How to use it

1. Add the node and open it in the Inspector. 2. Import a file, or switch to pins and click the map. 3. Check the column kinds. A column read as text when it holds numbers will not band or sum. 4. Open Data quality to see what is missing or malformed before you build on it. 5. Give the node a label that says what the records are, not where they came from.

What it will not do

It does not clean data silently. Nothing is coerced, dropped or filled in; what cannot be read is reported and left for you to decide.

It does not join one set of records to another. Two sets that share no key stay two sets.

It does not know what a row means. Whether 250 rows are 250 people or 250 addresses carrying 489 events is something your labels and your weights have to say.

Worked examples that use it

John Snow Voronoi catchments loads 250 death locations and eight pumps. Measles in Hagelloch, 1861 loads a 188-case line list. Old Naledi diagnostic access loads a facility registry.
polygon_input:
Polygon layer

An input widget. It supplies a layer of polygons — many areas, each with its own name and attributes — as distinct from a study area, which is the single boundary your work sits inside. Sub-districts, water bodies, supply zones, parishes, building footprints: anything that is a set of areas rather than one frame.

Two ways in

Choosing one shows that method's controls and hides the other, so the panel describes the path you are on.

A published GeoJSON layer. A FeatureCollection of polygons and multipolygons you already have. It is read exactly as published.

Areas from a published .osm.pbf extract. An OpenStreetMap extract — Geofabrik's country and region files, or any other — chosen with the file picker. You say which kinds of area you want and the widget reads those, within your study area's bounds.

What it does

It reads polygons into the workflow and emits them as a polygon layer, which maps, tables, charts and every polygon step already accept.

Read as published. Nothing is clipped, simplified or reprojected. A file whose coordinates are not longitude and latitude in degrees is refused rather than converted, because a converted shape is not the shape its author published.

Which property names each feature is yours to choose, and is never guessed from a property name. Leave it unset and the features are numbered. Name a property the file does not carry and the import is refused rather than silently leaving the names blank.

Reading from an extract needs a study area connected, because the study area is the scope: its bounds, widened by the margin you set, are the box the widget reads. The extract file is read where it sits and is never copied into this browser — only the areas it yields are kept, and they are kept on this device by digest rather than inside the workflow, so a large layer does not crowd out everything else you have saved.

Which kinds of area is a closed list, because each entry is a claim about which OpenStreetMap tags mean an area of that kind. Water covers lakes, rivers, basins and docks. Buildings covers anything tagged as a building. Nothing is matched on a feature's name.

A vertex threshold. A kind on its own is usually too coarse: water over a London-sized box returns about a thousand features, most of them ponds, basins and ornamental lakes. Setting a minimum number of vertices keeps the large features and leaves the small ones unread. If what you asked for is more than a layer can hold, the refusal tells you which threshold would fit, worked out from the features actually found rather than guessed, so the second attempt is informed.

The licence travels with the layer. Areas read from an OpenStreetMap extract are ODbL, which is share-alike: a figure built on them carries the same terms, and its credits must name OpenStreetMap. The panel and the run's receipt both say so, and the attribution is attached to the layer rather than remembered separately.

How to use it

From a file. Add the widget, leave the method on *A published GeoJSON layer*, and choose your file. The panel then shows how many features and vertices it read. If your features carry a name, type that property's name into *Which property names each feature* before you choose the file.

From an extract.

1. Add Study area and define it, then connect it on the widget's *Study area* control. The panel shows the box it will read from, so you can see what the margin does before anything is read. 2.
