Tick the kinds you want. 3. Set the margin if the features you need reach outside your bounds. A river's course, a reservoir or a lock can sit kilometres beyond the edge of a study area and still belong to the question. There is no ceiling: a larger box costs you a slower read, and the read is local. 4. If you do not have an extract, use the download button the panel offers. It names the smallest catalogued file that covers your box and your browser downloads it directly — this application cannot fetch it for you, because that host does not permit it. Come back to the file picker when it has landed. 5. Choose the file. The read runs in the background and reports each stage; the page stays usable while it works, which matters because a large extract takes several seconds at least. 6. Read what the panel says came back: how many features, how many vertices, how many were below your threshold, and how many fell outside the box. If the counts surprise you, change the threshold and read again.

Moving the study area afterwards. A layer read for one study area is refused for another: if the area grows past the box the layer was read for, the run stops and says so rather than drawing a map with a hole in it. Read the extract again. The file is not kept, so this means choosing it again — the panel records its name and digest so you know which file to look for.

What it will not do

It will not clip. The box decides which features are read, in or out; it never cuts one. A feature that crosses the edge of your study area arrives whole. Clipping is a separate step you choose and a receipt records.

It will not reproject. A layer in metres, a national grid or any projected system is refused. Convert it before you bring it in, so the conversion is yours and is recorded.

It will not find features by name. Searching an extract for "Thames" is not available, and is not an oversight: a name is not a reliable statement of what something is. You ask for a kind, and you get every area of that kind in the box.

It will not fetch an extract for you. The file has to be on your device. The widget works out which published file covers your box and links it; your browser does the downloading.

It will not keep the extract. Only the areas read out of it are kept. Reading again means choosing the file again.

How many features is not a limit. What refuses is vertices — two hundred thousand of them, because that is the thing that costs. A read of Greater London's water areas returns six hundred features and comes through. If a layer does pass the vertex budget, the refusal tells you which vertex floor would fit, read off the features the read actually found.

Choosing which features to keep

A read of a published extract gives you everything of the kinds you asked for inside your box. Greater London's water areas are 606 features; the Thames is two of them. The rest are ponds, basins and a boating lake.

Choose features opens a viewer: every feature the read returned, as a row, beside a map of all of them. Select a row and its polygon is marked on the map, so you can tell which one it is before deciding. Clear a row's box and that feature leaves the layer.

Nothing is deleted. The read is unchanged, so a feature you set aside comes back by ticking it again rather than by reading 124 MB a second time. The receipt records how many the read returned and how many you set aside, because a layer of two drawn from a read of 606 is a choice, and a reader of your evidence should be able to see that you made it.

Setting every feature aside is refused: a layer that holds nothing is not a layer.

Three reductions, and a name.

What it does
Keep or discardChoose features on the map or in the list, then keep only those or discard them. Or clear a single row's box.
Clip to the boxCut every feature to the box the read used. What falls wholly outside drops; what straddles the edge is cut at it.
MergeUnion the features you chose into one, keeping the group's first name. Two reaches of one river, or a dock drawn as four touching basins, are one thing your workflow counts once.

Adjacency is not checked before a merge. Features that do not touch become one feature of two parts, which is a real answer — a river above and below a lock is one river whether or not the data drew it sharing an edge — and refusing it would need a tolerance nobody has measured.

And you can name them. Type over any feature's name. A map whose polygons read "Feature 37" names nothing a reader can use, and the file does not always carry a property worth naming them by. Set aside the unnamed does it in bulk: it asks whether the property you nominated carried a value for each feature, never whether the name looks automatic.

All four are decisions applied when the workflow runs, not edits to the data. The read stays as it was published, so every one of them is reversible, and the receipt records what you chose.

*Why looking rather than typing:* the first design for this filtered at read time by a property name and a list of values. You cannot name values you have not seen, and nobody knows in advance what OpenStreetMap calls the boating lake.

Worked examples that use it

Snow's South London water supply study, 1854 reads the registration sub-districts and the two reaches of the Thames as layers inside one study area, which is what lets the tidal and non-tidal reaches be drawn as separate exposures.
rate:
Rate with a denominator

Counts divided by a population at risk, with what the population counts said. Cases per 100,000 people, deaths per 1,000 houses.

What it does

It divides a numerator, what was counted, by a denominator, the units at risk, for each group, and multiplies by 1, 100, 1,000, 10,000 or 100,000. The denominator's unit, the period the numerator covers and the vintage of the denominator travel with the result, because a rate whose denominator is unstated cannot be compared with any other.

What you connect

Records arrive as decides the input:

  • points, one per subject: each point carries the numerator and the denominator as attributes.
  • a table, in one of two forms, chosen under The table holds:

- one row per measure, named in a key column: Snow's South London table, where measure says population or deaths, or Brazil's, where variable says casos or pop. - both numbers on each row, as columns: Sierra Leone's cases by district, with the 2021 census brought beside each count by Relate a column from another table.

Changing Records arrive as disconnects the input, because points and a table are not the same shape. So choose it first, apply, then connect.

It gives back a table of groups and rates, which Join a table to the study area can map and Chart can draw.

How to use it

The step's panel holds its Name, its input, one sentence saying what it divides by what, and Configure…, where every setting is. The dialog's preview shows each group's numerator, denominator and rate before you apply, once the table can be read.

SettingWhat it decides
NumeratorWhat is counted: a measure's name, or a column
DenominatorThe units at risk: a measure's name, or a column
The denominator countspeople, houses, households, person-time, or other
Kindproportion, where the numerator is part of the denominator and cannot exceed it; or ratio, events per unit, which can
Per1 to 100,000
Group byThe column each rate is for, such as a district; none gives one rate for everything
Band widthFor a numeric grouping, the width of each band
Smallest denominator that gets a rateGroups below it report their counts and no rate
Period the numerator covers, Vintage of the denominatorRecorded and compared

What it will not do

  • It will not compute a rate from a value it cannot read. A row without a number for the numerator or the

denominator stops the run and names the row.

  • It will not let a proportion exceed one. That is a ratio, or a numerator that is not part of its denominator.
  • It will not give a rate for a small denominator. Below the stated minimum, a rate is unstable rather than

precise, so the counts are reported and the rate is not.

  • It will not decide whether the numerator's period and the denominator's vintage match. It records both; a

2019–2023 count over a 2021 census is a choice you state.

Where it is used

South London (deaths per 1,000 people, by sub-district), Brazil (notified cases per 100,000 residents, by municipality), and Sierra Leone (cases per 100,000 people by district, over the 2021 census).
relate_table:
Relate a column from another table

A join, narrowly. It takes two tables that name the same subjects, and brings a *category* from the second one onto the rows of the first.

What it does

Two tables often describe the same subjects and carry different things about them. John Snow's Table VIII gives each of 32 South London sub-districts its population and its cholera deaths; his Table XII gives each of the same 32 sub-districts the company that supplied its water. Neither table alone can answer *how many people died in the sub-districts supplied by one company*, and until this widget existed the application could not put them together — so the example repository carried that answer as a table somebody had computed by hand.

Relating Table XII's water_supply onto Table VIII gives every row a supply category. Nothing is added up yet; that is the next step.

What you connect

PortWhat goes there
recordsthe table being added to
relatedthe table being read from

Both are tables. The order matters: the first keeps its rows and gains a column, the second is only read.

How to use it

The step's panel holds four things: its Name, its two Inputs (*Table being added to* and *Table read from*), one sentence saying what it will do, and Configure…. After a run it says, in one line, how many rows related and which were dropped. Under that, Manual, Evidence and Version, then Duplicate and Remove.

Configure… opens the step's dialog, where everything is set. It has three parts, top to bottom:

  • Settings, below;
  • Preview: the join these settings would make, before anything is applied;
  • Decisions: what happens to rows that did not match, which the step will not choose for you.

Nothing changes the workflow until Apply. Cancel, × and the Escape key leave the step as it was; if you have changed something, the dialog asks before discarding it.

SettingWhat it decides
Matched on, in the first tablethe column holding the names or codes, such as sub_district
The same, in the second tablethe second table's column for them; the column of the same name where there is one. A line list's Residential District against a population's district
And also matched onmore shared columns, where one column does not identify a subject: a monitor's reading is one row per site and date. A row relates only where every chosen column agrees
Bring acrossthe second table's column to add, such as water_supply, or its value column, such as a monitor's reading in ppb or a district's census population, which arrives as written and as a number, with its unit, so Rate with a denominator can divide by it
Compare keysfolding punctuation and case; exactly after trimming; or allowing for spelling, and dropping words
A date within a periodoptional; see below
Shifts, in daysoptional; see below

Compare keys

Two sources spell names differently. Snow's own tables agree with each other, because both transcribe the same book — but his sub-district names against the published boundaries match 23 of 32 exactly and 32 of 32 once punctuation is folded, and every one of the nine differences is a single comma. So folding is the default, and the choice is recorded in the evidence.

Tighten it to exactly when a punctuation difference means two different subjects. Loosen it when it means one subject written twice.

Allowing for spelling, and dropping words. Sources also differ by more than punctuation. A line list writes "Bo District" where the boundaries write "Bo", and "Falaba District" where they write "Fabala". With this chosen:

  • Words to drop are taken out of both columns before comparing, as whole words: District takes "Bo District"

to "bo", and leaves "Districtville" alone. Separate several with commas.

  • Spelling allowed is the similarity a name must reach to match one spelled differently: 0.88 to start, from

0.5 to 1. Higher allows fewer differences; 1 allows none. It is Jaro-Winkler, as Deduplicate records uses.

Each name is matched once. The preview lists every name, how it was compared, what it matched and how: matched exactly, matched allowing for spelling with its score, ambiguous where two names are as close, or not found. An ambiguous name is listed under Decisions with its candidates: choose one, or none. A name not found, or left undecided, is an unmatched row, decided as any is.

The result gains a column saying how each row matched, such as Residential District match. You can bring the second table's own column across, such as district, to have its spelling on every row.

Check the spelling matches in the preview. A close spelling is not always the same place: "Fabala" is Falaba because the boundaries hold no other district like it, which you can see and the step cannot.

The preview

The dialog's Preview shows three things, and they change together as you choose:

1. The shape of the join — a bar of the keys only in the first table, in both, and only in the second. Keys, not rows: a table here holds several rows per subject, so counting rows would say that nine unmatched sub-districts are eighteen unmatched things. 2. The effect on each numeric variable — what each one totals over the whole table, over the rows that matched, and the share retained. Read this before anything else; see below. 3. The Methods note this step will machine, and a preview of the table that will travel on, with the key columns marked Matched on and the column added Brought across, as in View this table.

Then Apply. Nothing is written until you press it.

What the shares are telling you

If two variables keep different shares, the rows that did not match are not a random sample of what you are measuring. On Snow's Table VIII against the published boundaries, 68.2% of population is retained against 61.2% of deaths — so a mortality rate computed on the matched rows comes out at 89.6% of its value over the whole table, 2.787 per 1000 against 3.109.

That multiplier is arithmetic and not an estimate: a rate of one variable over another is multiplied by exactly the ratio of their retained shares. It runs backwards too. If the figure you expected and the figure you are looking at differ by that ratio, you are looking at a number produced by a join you did not intend — and the shares say which one.

Had both variables kept the same share, the exclusion would cost precision and leave the estimate alone.

The rows that did not match

Where any key of the first table has no row in the second, the step will not run until you say what to do, under Decisions in the dialog. Neither choice is ticked to begin with: the two answers give different totals and the result cannot be read for which one you got, so nothing here chooses for you.

ChoiceWhat you get
Drop themonly the matched rows, and the totals the shares describe
Keep them under a category I nameevery row, and the totals of the whole first table

Keeping needs a name, and it has to be yours — nothing here will invent a stratum the data never measured, and a name already used by the second table is refused so that unmeasured rows cannot join a measured group.

Your decision is stored with a signature of the gap it was made about. Edit either table, or change how keys are compared, and the decision lapses rather than riding on data it was not made about.

Why it brings a category and not a number

A table in this application is long: it has key columns, which hold labels, and one value column, which holds numbers. A water supply company is a label, so it can only arrive as a key column — and a key column lands on every row, which is why the row count does not change.

Bringing *numbers* across would mean adding rows instead, and that is a different operation with a different way of going wrong: two tables can disagree about the same measure. It is not built.

A date within a period, and a lag

Some tables do not share a date. Weekly cases have a week; a satellite product has an 8-day period with a start and an end. Match a date within a period relates each row to the row of the second table whose start and end hold its date, alongside the columns matched on as usual (the municipality, say).

SettingWhat it decides
Date, in the first tablethe date to place, such as data_iniSE, the Sunday a week starts
Period start and Period end, in the secondthe span each row of the second table covers
Shifts, in days+ Add a shift, then the days added to the date before it is placed: +3 takes a week's Sunday to its Wednesday, and a lag of *k* weeks is 7*k* days fewer, so a 2-week lag from the Wednesday is −11

The result keeps the shifted date and the matched period's start on every row, so each match can be checked. A date that falls inside two periods of the second table, such as two satellites' rows for one period, is refused by name: keep one row per period first. A date in no period is a row with no match, decided as any other.

Several shifts in one step. Add two or more shifts and the column is brought once per shift, each as a column of its own named by the shift: LST_Day_1km_-11d, LST_Day_1km_-25d. Every row is kept. A row with no value at a shift has that column left empty, and the preview and the run count the empties per shift. So there is no decision about unmatched rows to make: nothing is dropped. Several shifts need a date within a period, each a whole number of days, none listed twice. There is no limit on how many: each shift takes about half a second on 77,740 rows.

A table can be related to itself, shifted. Rainfall two weeks before each case week is the weekly table's own rainfall, 14 days earlier: choose the week's start as the date, the period's start and its end. The first table already has that column, so the matched week is written as data_iniSE_matched and the first table's own date is kept. A second shift on a table that already holds one is written as data_iniSE_shifted_2, beside the first.

A decision about unmatched rows is kept as a short digest of the rows it was made about, so it lapses when they change. Sixteen years of weekly cases left 58,401 rows unmatched in one join; the decision used to be stored with all of them written out, and seven such joins filled the browser's storage. A decision saved that way before 0.41.0 still holds.

Reading what you get

The same table with one more column, and, on the step after a run, one line saying what the join did: for example *4 of 6 rows related; 2 dropped, with no district in supply.csv: Charlie.*

Read the dropped count first. A row that found no match is absent from the table that travels on, so the result is internally consistent whether it holds all of your rows or two thirds of them. The line names the keys that did not match, so you can go and look at the second table rather than only know that something is missing. Where nothing was dropped it says so, because "none" is the claim you need and a zero is easy to pass over. With several shifts, the line counts the empty rows per shift instead.

View this table repeats the column origins above each column heading, so a wide related table says which half of the row came from where. It also marks the join's own columns: each key column Matched on, tinted, in every *Before* and in *After*, and the column added Brought across in *After*.

The Methods note

This step machines a note for the Methods section of a write-up: what was brought from where, on what key, compared how, how many keys appeared in both tables, and — where rows were excluded — which keys those were and what share of each variable survived. A join is a thing you did to the data, and the count of what it excluded is Methods prose in an epidemiology paper rather than a limitation.

The dialog's preview shows the note each choice would produce, so you can read the sentence before applying it. The run records it in the evidence.

What it will not do

  • It will not choose between two answers. If the second table gives one key two different

values of the column being brought across, this refuses and names the key. Taking the first would produce a grouping that is wrong in a way no total reveals, and the ambiguity is usually telling you the key does not identify what you think it identifies.

  • It will not invent a category. A key the second table has no row for is reported by name

and those rows are dropped. Filling in "unknown" would put a stratum in your table that nobody measured.

  • It will not match approximately unless you ask. Keys are compared exactly after trimming, or with

punctuation and case folded, unless you choose allowing for spelling (see Compare keys). Even then it will not choose between two names equally close: you do.

  • It will not allow for spelling on a date within a period. Choose one or the other.
  • It will not tell you the two tables describe the same subjects. That is your judgement. The

widget checks that the keys line up, not that they mean the same thing.

Where it is used

The South London example: *Died or survived, by water supply*. The NYC example: *Did the satellite see the city's NO₂?*, which matches satellite and ground readings on site and date together and brings the ground reading, the second table's value, across.

How it was checked

Validation Lab check 28, 28-relate-table-vs-pandas.ipynb, against a pandas left merge of Snow's Table XII onto his Table VIII. There is no arithmetic to check, so what was recomputed is the matching: the same category on the same row, the row count unchanged at 64, and the same rows dropped and named when a sub-district is withheld.

The case worth an outside eye is the ambiguous key. A merge resolves it by multiplying rows — 66 rows out of a 64-row table — so the sub-district's population would appear under both companies with no total revealing it. This refuses instead, and the check records the merge's row count as the measure of what the refusal prevents.

What it does not reach: Snow's two tables spell every sub-district identically, so a name differing by punctuation or case — the case you will actually meet — is never exercised.
append_rows:
Append rows

A summary step. It stacks the rows of two or more tables, one after another, as pandas concat does.

What it does

Two or more tables become one, with every row of each, in the order of the ports. Columns are lined up by name. A column some tables lack is empty on their rows, and the run says which column, which table and how many rows, because empty there means the question was not asked.

What you connect

PortWhat goes there
recordsthe first table, whose rows come first
records_2the second table, whose rows follow
records_3, ...each further table, added with ＋ Add a table in the Inspector

How to use it

SettingWhat it decides
Name the source of each rowAdds a column holding a label for each table's rows
Column naming the sourceThat column's name, source unless you change it
＋ Add a table and Remove the last tableHow many tables it stacks: one port each, two at least
Label for rows of each tableWhat that column holds on that table's rows
The labels are numbers, and Their unitSays the labels are numbers, such as a lag in weeks, so a chart places them as numbers and titles its axis with the unit
Create a new primary keyAdds a column numbering every row 1 to N, and makes it the primary key

When the old keys would repeat

Each table's own id is unique, but two tables stacked can share an id. Where both declare the same primary key, the stacked table's key is:

Options onPrimary keyAlso unique
Neitherthe old key; any repeat is a Data quality finding
Source namedsource with the old key
New keythe new key
Source named and new keythe new keysource with the old key

The old key column is always kept.

The Salmonella example stacks 32 cases, selected from the complete file, on the 81 matched panel controls from the second file, so the two-by-two can compare them.

Many tables, one step

Five models, one per lag, are five tables. One Append rows stacks them all: add a port for each with ＋ Add a table, rather than chaining four steps. The Brazil dengue example stacks five Regression tables this way and labels each table's rows with its lag, 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8.

The labels are numbers only when you say so. Nothing is read off the labels. A label that is not a number, such as 2 weeks, is a data quality finding naming its rows, and the rows are kept. A chart cannot place those on a numeric axis.

An estimate's interval, declared by Regression, survives the stacking when every table declares it the same way, so Chart can draw each estimate with its interval.

What it will not do

  • Stack tables whose value columns or units differ. They measure different things, and one column cannot mean both.
  • Use a source column name any table already has, or one label for two tables.
  • Check that the two tables were collected the same way. Two surveys with different questions stack without

complaint if their value column has one name.

  • Find a primary key repeated across the tables.
  • Read a label as a number unless you say the labels are numbers.
select_rows:
Select rows by value

A selection. It keeps the rows whose chosen column holds one of the values you name, in the order you name them, and drops the rest.

What it does

What a figure should show is often less than what a table carries. After *Derive a value* computes houses without a death, Snow's Table IX holds three measures — houses, deaths and houses without a death — and only the last two belong in a 2×2, because houses is the total the other two partition. Leaving it in gives the grid a third column and a totals row that counts every house twice.

Keeping deaths and houses without a death leaves exactly the 2×2, and its totals come out as the houses supplied.

Seeing what this step did

The Inspector says in one sentence what the step keeps, such as *Keeps the rows with date from 2023-06-01 to 2023-06-14, both ends included*, and after a run, in one line, how many rows it kept and left out, and any value named that the table does not hold.

View this table at the top of the Inspector opens the output. Before and After switch between the table that came in and the one that went out, and After says how many rows and columns there were before.

What you connect

records — a table. It gives back the same table with fewer rows. Key columns, value field and unit are unchanged, because selecting rows does not change what a table measures.

How to use it

Configure… in the Inspector opens the step's settings. They show what they keep as you change them: how many rows of how many, and the table. Nothing changes until Apply; Cancel, × or Escape leave the step as it was, and ask first if you changed something.

SettingWhat it decides
Key column to choose byWhich column the values belong to.
KeepThe values I tick, Every value except those I tick, or A range of dates (or numbers). The range is offered only when every value in the column is a date, or every one a number.
Values to keepTicked from the values on offer, or typed one per line. A list of more than 12 can be searched, and Ticked only shows what you have kept.
From and ToThe range. Both ends are kept; leave one empty to run from the start or to the end.

Leaving values out keeps the table's order, and every row whose value is not one of those ticked. The Brazil sixteen-year workflow leaves out the twelve weeks the file holds twice, with twelve ticks instead of 821. A value ticked that the table does not hold is reported, as when keeping.

A range keeps the table's order, and a row with no value in the column is outside every range. For 1 to 14 June 2023 out of ten years of days, that is two fields instead of fourteen ticks. Dates compare as dates written year-month-day; numbers as numbers, so 9 comes before 10. A column of names gets no range, because any order for it would be one the application made up.

Order matters. The rows come out in the order you name the values, so a 2×2 reads the way you asked for rather than the way the file happened to be written. Unticking a value and ticking it again moves it to the end, which is how you reorder without a second control.

What it refuses, and why

A value the table does not hold is reported, not ignored. Asking for a row that is not there is usually a typo, or a table upstream that changed. Quietly returning fewer rows than you asked for is how a figure loses a category nobody noticed.

Keeping nothing the table holds is refused in the settings, where Apply waits until it is changed, rather than handing back an empty table. So is a range that keeps nothing, which says where the column runs from and to; a range written backwards; and an end that is not a date, or not a number, when the column holds those.

What it will not do

It will not tell you whether what you kept is a fair selection. Dropping the categories that disagree with you looks exactly like dropping a double-counted total. Decide which you are doing, and say so where a reader can see it.

It will not add a value that is missing. Naming a value the table does not hold leaves it out and reports it; it does not create an empty category to hold a place in a figure.

It will not change what the rows mean. The unit, the value field and the key columns are the table's, and they come back as they went in.

What this does not establish

That a selection is an honest one. Keeping a subset of categories is exactly how a figure misleads, and this widget cannot tell a partition from a cherry-pick: it will drop the rows that disagree with you as readily as the ones that double-count. The evidence records which values were kept and how many rows went, so the choice is at least visible to a reader.
snap_to_network:
Snap to network

A process widget. It moves each of your sites onto the nearest junction of a street network, so that steps which travel along streets have somewhere to start.

What it does

A route has to begin on the street network. Your sites almost never sit exactly on a junction — a pump is in a yard, a clinic is set back from the road — so this widget finds the nearest junction to each one and puts it there.

It also records how far each site moved, which is the number to watch.

What you connect

ConnectWhat it needs
your sitesthe points to move
a street networkfrom the Street network widget

Out come the same sites, at junctions, each carrying the distance it travelled. Feed them to Reachable junctions or a walking-catchment step.

How to use it

1. Add it from the palette, under Catchments. 2. Connect your sites and a street network. 3. Set the snap limit — how far a site may be from the network before the result says so. 4. Run the workflow, then read the snap distances in the output or the Inspector.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat it does there
John Snow · walking catchmentsputs the eight pumps onto the Soho street network before travel times are computed

What it will not do

  • It will not leave your data where it was. Every site comes out at a junction. The output

is derived data, not observations any more, and the furthest any site moved is recorded in the run evidence.

  • It will not drop a site that is far from the network. A site past the snap limit is still

moved to its nearest junction and is marked: its first leg crosses ground no street covers. The widget glows red on the canvas and the Inspector lists each one with its distance. The limit decides whether the result says so, not whether the site is in it.

  • It will not tell you the move was acceptable. If a site travelled 200 m to reach a

junction, everything measured afterwards starts 200 m from where it should, and that error appears nowhere in the final numbers. Check the snap distance every time.

When sites are marked, you have three honest options: raise the limit, extend the street network where it stops short, or accept the list and say so in what you publish.

Checking it yourself

The lab's snapping notebook checks the junction choice against pyproj and measures each displacement against a five-minute walking budget — one of the eight example pumps was decided by 0.43 m.
study_area:
Study area

An input widget. It defines where your work takes place: one shape, kept on this device, that every later step can be scoped to.

What it does

A study area holds one piece of geography and makes it available to the rest of the workflow. You can draw it, or take it from a published administrative boundary.

Drawn. A bounding box, a polygon you click out, or a circle around a point. Quick, and it is yours — nothing outside the workflow knows what it means.

A drawn shape cannot be fetched by anybody else, so the thing worth recording about it is who drew it. If a GitHub login is set on the area, the receipt names that person as the author of the geometry and says whether the login was simply entered here or confirmed by GitHub. With no login set, nobody is named: the receipt reports the shape and leaves the author blank rather than assuming it was whoever opened the file. This also applies if you take a published boundary and then move it — the source is credited for what the shape came from, and you are credited for the shape.

From a boundary source. Chosen by country and level from geoBoundaries: ADM1 is usually a province or region, ADM2 a district or city, and what each level means differs by country. The level is checked before anything is downloaded, so you see how many units there are and how detailed they are before committing. You then pick the units you want, and the shape you get is the one the source published, vertex for vertex.

The shape is stored in longitude, latitude order (CRS84). Applying it writes N3 facts you can read in the N3 & evidence tab.

What you connect

It has no input. Its output is an area, which the map, the buffer, the raster window, the facility search, the point grid, the coverage check and the area measurement all accept.

How to use it

The step's panel holds its Name, one sentence saying what shape it holds, the Country where it was not taken from a boundary, and Select area on map, which opens the map where the area is chosen. Result says what it holds, what the boundary repair removed, and every extent it has had. Under that, Manual, Evidence and Version.

1. Add the node and open it in the Inspector. 2. Press Select area on map. Pan to where you are working. 3. Either draw — Bounding box, Polygon or Point and radius — or open Use an administrative boundary, enter a country, pick a level, press Check this level, and choose the units you need. Or open Use a boundary file you already have, name the property holding each boundary's name, and choose a GeoJSON file. 4. Press Apply study area. 5. Give it a label that says what it is. The label travels into the receipts.

Changing the shape later keeps the old one: the Inspector lists every extent you have kept and restores any of them, which records a new extent carrying the old shape rather than overwriting anything.

The boundary repair

Published boundaries sometimes carry two faults that change no outline, and that this step would otherwise refuse:

FaultWhat is removed
A point written twice in a rowThe second copy
A zero-width spike: the outline goes out along a line and comes straight back along itThe vertex at the tip

Neither changes the area any outline encloses. Every other vertex is kept as published. The repair runs on every boundary as it is read, a downloaded level or a file, and the dialog says what it removed, by district for a spike.

It is recorded, so it can be redone. The evidence says how many of the published vertices were removed, by this rule, and lists each one by unit, kind and position. OCHA's districts of Sierra Leone are the case it was found on: 84 repeated vertices across 14 districts, and one spike about a metre long in Bonthe.

A ring that touches itself anywhere else is not repaired, and is still refused, because that is a different shape.

What it will not do

It does not simplify a boundary you took from a source. A published polygon is a claim about where a jurisdiction is, and thinning it would quietly change that claim. The boundary repair above removes only what encloses no area, and says so.

It does not fetch data by itself. It says *where*; a source widget says *what*.

A drawn shape is not a jurisdiction. If your result needs to be about a named place, take the boundary from a source so the receipt can say whose line it is.

Several selected units stay several shapes. They are not merged into one outline and never become a bounding box around the group.

It does not refuse units that share a border, or rings that meet at a single point, such as an island touching another at a corner or a hole touching its outline. Both are valid shapes, and Brazil's municipalities have them. It refuses shapes whose interiors overlap, and rings that cross or run along each other.

Worked examples that use it

Old Naledi · diagnostic access uses a drawn settlement boundary. Old Naledi · raster clipping scopes a population raster to the same shape. The four 1854 Cholera Outbreak in London workflows each use their own Soho extent, which is why three of them differ.
summarize_combined_area:
Combined area

Takes areas and gives back one area, or takes polygons and gives back one polygons result. It combines whatever kind it is given, and hands back the same kind.

What it does

Given two study areas — say two adjacent provinces — it carries both outlines through as the parts of one study area. That area can then be given to everything a study area feeds: the street network, the facility sources, the clip, the buffer.

Given a polygons result — catchments, hulls, buffers — it dissolves the ones that overlap or touch into single polygons and leaves separate ones separate, in a metric projection you choose.

What you connect

portwhat it takes
polygonsa polygons result, to dissolve
area and area2two study areas, to combine

Every port is always there. What the widget *yields* follows what you wire: connect areas and the output is an area; connect polygons and it is a polygons result. Nothing to set.

How to use it

To combine two study areas. Add the widget, then connect one study area to area and the other to area2. The output becomes an area the moment the first one is wired, so it can be given to a Street network, a facility source, a clip or a buffer exactly as a single study area would be. Name it if you want; unnamed, it takes the parts' names joined with a plus.

To dissolve a polygons result. Connect it to polygons and set the metric zone and hemisphere for the projection the dissolve is computed in. Overlapping and touching polygons become one; separate ones stay separate, and the count of each is reported.

What it assumes

That a touching border should not be dissolved when combining areas. Two provinces that share a border come through as two parts, not one welded outline. A published outline is an authority's record of where a boundary lies; two authorities describe a shared border differently, and welding them would assert a third line that neither drew while still citing both as the source. Every question this application asks of a study area — is this point inside, what does an extract clip to, what are the bounds — is answered identically by two parts. What they do not do is pretend the border is gone.

That dissolving IS right for polygons. A catchment is this application's own construction, not somebody's record of where a line is, so two that overlap are one reachable region and are merged.

That the first area's spatial reference is the combination's. Combining areas held in different projections is a question nobody has asked here yet, and guessing an answer would bury it.

What it will not do

  • It will not dissolve areas, for the reason above.
  • It will not combine an area with a polygons result. They are different kinds and the output

would have to be one of them.

  • It will not reproject. The metric projection on the polygons path is yours to set; the area path

carries the first part's reference through unchanged.

What the receipt says

On the area path: fw:AreaCombination as the activity, prov:used for each part, fw:partCount, and fw:ringCount on the geometry — so a reader can see the parts were kept rather than merged.

Checked against

The polygons path is checked against shapely/GEOS in the validation lab (12-combined-area, agrees: combined area 701,662.61 m² against 701,662.61 m², zero symmetric difference). That check covers the polygons path only. The area path, added 2026-10-22, has no external check yet, and no Dive Deeper lesson — those are two different repositories and two different questions: the lab recomputes what this widget computed, and a lesson teaches what the method IS.
summarize_hull:
Observed extent (convex hull)

A process widget. It takes points and gives back one polygon: the smallest convex outline that contains them, with the area it encloses.

What it does

Stretch an elastic band around all your points and let it go. The shape it settles into is the convex hull — the outline of where your observations are, with no dents.

Along with the shape you get two measurements the rest of your workflow can read: the area it encloses, in square metres, and its span, the distance across its longest axis.

What you connect

ConnectWhat it needs
a point layerat least three points that have locations

Out comes one polygon. Connect it to a Map to see it, a Table to read its numbers, or a Ruleset to make a judgement about its size.

How to use it

1. Add it from the palette, under Summaries. 2. Connect a point layer. Points without a location sit the step out, and the notes say how many took part. 3. Check the zone. The widget measures in metres, so it projects your points first, and the UTM zone it uses is part of the answer. The Inspector suggests the zone that fits your data and tells you what a different one would cost. 4. Run the workflow, then read the area on the output or draw the outline on a map.

Worked examples that use it

ExampleWhat it does there
John Snow · outbreak extentoutlines the 250 death locations, and a ruleset judges whether the outbreak extent is large enough to look at

What it will not do

  • It will not follow the shape of your data. A hull is convex, and cases along a river or

facilities along a coast are not. The outline fills in the space between them, so it claims ground where nothing was observed. If that matters, do not use a hull.

  • It is not a boundary. It is an outline of what was *seen* — not a service area, not a

catchment, not anything anyone agreed to. Where your observation stopped is not where the thing you were observing stopped.

  • Three points in a line enclose nothing, and the widget refuses rather than returning an

area of zero.

  • Watch the span against the area. A hull much longer than it is wide is close to a line

and should be read as one. The widget says so in its notes when it happens.

Checking it yourself

The lab's hull notebook recomputes the outline and the area with Shapely and compares them to this widget's.
table_input:
Tabular data

A source. It reads a CSV, Excel or Stata file into a table.

What it does

It reads a CSV, Excel (.xlsx) or Stata (.dta) file in wide or long shape and hands a table to the next step. An absent value is kept as unknown, never read as zero.

How to use it

The Inspector says in one sentence what the step reads: the file, its shape, its value columns and its unit. Configure… opens the import.

1. Choose the file, and say whether it is wide or long. 2. Tick the key columns and choose the value column or columns. 3. Under What identifies a row?, mark any primary and secondary keys. 4. Apply. Nothing changes until you do; Cancel or × leaves the step as it was.

After it, the Inspector's Result says how many rows were read and how many values are absent, what Data quality found, and how many columns are described, with Quick look at the table, Data quality and Describe columns…. If it names a Data quality finding, open it before relying on the table.

Convert the source table on each run, in the dialog, keeps the file as published and melts it when the workflow runs, so the run's receipt names the columns it took. It can be changed without reading the file again.

Excel workbooks

A workbook of several sheets offers Sheet: choose the one holding the table, and it is set up as a CSV is. The dialog says which sheet it read, and the step keeps it, so a table fetched again reads the same sheet. Cells are read as written: a formula gives its saved result, and formatting is ignored, so a date Excel stores as a number stays that number. An older .xls file needs saving as .xlsx or CSV first.

Stata files

A Stata file, from Stata 8 onward, is read as Stata wrote it and then set up as a CSV is. Numbers are as stored. A missing value, . or .a to .z, is empty, never zero. A variable Stata formats as a date is read as a date. Value labels are not applied: codes stay as stored, and the import says which variables carry labels.

Fetched from a URL

Under Or fetch from a URL, give the address of a CSV, a Stata file or a zip. For a zip, choose the file inside. The table is then set up as any other.

The project keeps where the table came from, the URL, the file inside and the digests, in place of its rows. An exported project carries no rows, so sharing it does not republish data whose terms do not allow that. On another device the step says its rows are not fetched yet, and Fetch the table, under Settings, reads the same file again with the same settings. A file whose digest has changed is refused, and nothing is read.

Downloaded once per device. What is fetched is kept on the device by its digest. Any table, in any project on the device, that names the same file reads it from there, checked again, instead of downloading it. Typed again in the dialog, a URL reads the copy and says when it was fetched; Fetch again from the source checks for a newer file. A source that has not finished after two minutes is stopped and said to be late.

Keys

A file with more than 12 columns lists them in a dialog of its own: Key columns shows how many are ticked and which, and Choose key columns… opens the list, with Columns to keep (paste or type names, separated by commas, then Keep these), Find a column, Untick all and Ticked only. A name the file does not have is said. Read long, such a file starts with nothing ticked; a smaller one ticks every column but the value, and lists them inline. Value columns, for a wide read, work the same way.

Key columns are read as labels. Among them you decide what identifies a row:

DeclarationMeansChecked
Primary keyOne column or several together are uniqueYes
Secondary keyGroups or links rows, and may repeatNo
NeitherAn answer or categoryNo

With no primary key declared, the check is on all the key columns together.

List the distinct values of ticks key columns whose values the table lists, for a step that needs them as a list. Assign projection site reads the sites it assigns against from site_id here, so tick it on the projections table. Nothing else changes: the rows are the same.

What the columns mean

Describe columns… on the node opens a dialog for every column the table keeps: a label, a unit and a description. The column's name stays as the file spells it; the label is shown beside it, in a regression's terms and a chart's panels. Describing the columns is your step, and a data quality check: a column nobody has described is a finding in Data quality and in the write-up's Methods, never a reason to refuse the table.

From a data dictionary. Under *Propose from a data dictionary*, choose a CSV, Excel workbook or Stata file with one row per variable, or, for a table fetched from a zip, a file in the same archive (read from this device). Say which of its columns holds the variable name, label, description, unit and missing count; a first guess from its headers is filled in. Propose descriptions fills the columns it describes, marked *not yet accepted*, and checks it against the table: which kept columns it does not describe, and whether each missing count it states agrees with the table's. Accept each proposal, or Accept every proposal; typing in a field makes the description yours.

A Stata file's own variable labels are proposed the same way when it is imported.

Data quality

A file is not refused for a quality problem. Every row is kept, the step's Result names what Data quality found, and the Findings tab of Data quality lists:

  • rows repeating a key value
  • rows with no value in a key column
  • values that are not numbers, kept as unknown and never as zero

A finding left unresolved goes into the write-up as a machined limitation.

A file with no rows, too many rows or a missing column is still refused, because there is no table to look at.

Read as wide, a repeated subject is kept. When the key columns repeat a subject, the dialog says the file may be long and offers to read it so. Usually it is. But a wide file can repeat a subject because the source has a fault, and the Brazil dengue file has one week twice for every municipality. Read as wide anyway, every row is kept and each repeat is a finding in Data quality.

What it will not do

It does not choose between rows that disagree. The table stays as read until a later step changes it.
table_output:
Table

What it does

Shows what you connect to it, as a table in its own Results tab.

It takes four different things, and it works out which it is showing from what you wire:

  • a keyed table from any step that produces one — Relate a column, Total within groups, a rate,

a two-by-two, an imported table;

  • point data, with coordinates and attributes;
  • catchment polygons and their summaries;
  • reasoning results, with their decisions.

What you connect

Every port is on the node from the moment you add it. There is nothing to choose first.

Connect a step's output to the matching port and the table shows it. If you wire more than one, the more specific wins: a keyed table before polygons, polygons before decisions, and the point path is the general one.

How to use it

1. Add it, or use Quick Look on a step and open its table from there. 2. Drag from the step's output to the port that matches what it produces, or choose it under Inputs. 3. Name the Results tab.

The step's panel holds its Name and where it goes in the write-up, its Inputs, one sentence saying what it shows, Configure…, and what the last run showed.

In Configure…When it is offered
Show totals: these values count the same thingA keyed table that states no unit. Tick it only where every cell counts the same thing; the figure says you asserted it
Display as: Table, Map or ChartA reasoning result. Map or Chart changes the step into that output

Nothing is required. A table with nothing connected is unfinished, not broken, and says so.

A column that holds a number, such as a projection Relate brought beside each row, is always drawn as a column with its own heading, even where every row holds the same number.

It states its own shape in the write-up

Every run machines a note into Results on the Notes tab stating what this table is made of. It names the columns as the table spells them, says how many rows, reports empty cells as unknown rather than zero, and names the source file and digest where the table came in as a file. Only in the table mode: the point, polygon and decision views are not published tables.

Column names are shown as they are, in code, rather than bent into a sentence. A generator cannot tell whether measure or group is a noun, so it states them and leaves the prose to you.

The caption is yours. A caption states the subject, the population, the place and the period in your words, and none of that can be read off a table. What this writes is what the table declares about itself — the material you write the caption from, sitting beside it in the same section.

And it carries no number. A figure's number depends on where it sits in the write-up and on the venue you are preparing — set one figure aside and the ones after it move up — so the number is worked out when the document is rendered. Nothing here says "Figure 1".

Edit it and it forks into a note of your own, like any machined note; the machined one goes on being rewritten by every run.

Where it goes in the write-up

In the write-up, under, just below Results tab name in the panel, chooses the part of the Notes write-up this output's figure and its note go in: Introduction, Methods, Results or Discussion. Results is the default. A map of the study area belongs in the Introduction; a figure that shows how the analysis was done can go in Methods. References is not offered, because it holds works and not figures. The run's receipt states the section and whether you chose it, and a validation rule checks that the note describing the figure is filed in that same section.

What it will not do

  • It will not ask you what shape your data is. There is no mode to set, and connecting

something never removes a connection you already made. Map works the same way.

  • It will not chart the table. Charting one means choosing which key varies and whether to

aggregate, which is a decision rather than a port. Use Chart.

  • It will not total anything you have not said can be added. Margins appear only with Show totals. To total

rows into groups, use Total within groups.

Where it is used

The South London example, five times: the mortality rate table, both water-company tables and both contingency tables.

How it was checked

Unit tests over the port list, the renderer the connections imply, and the fallback to a stored mode for a workflow saved before the mode was removed. One pins the defect directly: a freshly added table offers a table port with no mode set.

What no test establishes is whether the four renderers should be one widget at all. The split is inherited and is recorded as open in [experiment 21](../experiments/21-shared-result-outputs.md).
study_design:
Study design

A workflow declares HOW as well as WHERE. study_area says where a study is; nothing said what kind of study it is. This declares the design and the study period, and states which measures that design can actually support.

What it does

It computes nothing. It declares one of five designs and the period the study covers, and the computations downstream find it by walking upstream from themselves.

DesignWhat one row countsWhat a two-by-two may estimate under it
cohorta personrisk, risk ratio, risk difference, odds ratio
case-controla personthe odds ratio only
cross-sectionala personprevalence, prevalence ratio, prevalence odds ratio
ecologicala groupthe same measures, as group-level quantities
case-seriesa personcounts and intervals — no comparison group, so no ratio

Five, not the twenty-two of the reference survey. Each is one this application can actually serve with the widgets it has; a sixth that licensed no computation would be a declaration doing no work.

Why case-control is the one that matters

In a cohort you sample people and follow them, so the row totals a+b and c+d are populations at risk and a/(a+b) is a risk.

In a case-control study you choose how many cases and how many controls to sample. The row totals are then artefacts of that choice — sample twice as many controls and a+b doubles while nothing about the disease changes. So a/(a+b) is not a risk, and the risk ratio and risk difference built from it are not estimable at all. The odds ratio survives because the cross-product ad/bc does not depend on how many of each group were sampled.

Without a declared design, a case-control table is offered all three. The arithmetic is right and two of the three answers mean nothing.

What the odds ratio then means depends on how the controls were sampled — and this widget does not ask. Under incidence-density (risk-set) sampling an odds ratio estimates an incidence rate ratio without needing the outcome to be rare; under cumulative sampling it does not. So declaring case-control is enough to rule the risk measures out, and not enough to say which ratio the surviving one is. Record how you sampled controls in the note field until there is a field for it.

Cross-sectional is the quieter failure. There the arithmetic keeps its value and loses its name: a/(a+b) is a prevalence, not a risk, and a prevalence ratio printed as Risk Ratio (RR) is correct to three decimals and wrong about what it measures. Nothing looks amiss, which is why it is the worse of the two.

Ecological is the inference, not the arithmetic. The rows count groups. South London's contingency workflow attaches a water company to each of 32 sub-districts, so every measure over it is a statement about sub-districts — and a relation between group-level measures need not hold between individuals.

The study period

Declared here because it belongs to the study, not to a computation. rate carries a numeratorPeriod and a denominatorVintage, and case_series carries a period, all of which are properties of one calculation — which is backwards for a title, whose time element is the period of the study.

Written as it should read: 1854, or July–September 1854.

How a computation finds it

By walking upstream from itself. A design wired by an edge wins outright, because an edge is an explicit statement; otherwise the walk looks back through the graph.

Three consequences worth knowing:

  • Upstream only. A design declared downstream of a computation did not govern it, and a design

on a parallel branch governs that branch and not this one.

  • Two different designs are refused, never resolved. Which study you are running is not a tie

this application may break. Two nodes *agreeing* on one design is fine — what cannot be resolved is two answers to one question.

  • relate_table, group_table, derive_value and select_rows carry nothing. The walk

passes through them, so a declaration does not have to be threaded along a chain.

How to use it

1. Add it before the computations it governs. It takes no input, so it sits at the start of a branch the way a study area does. 2. Choose the design and its measures. The dialog shows what each design licenses before you choose it. What it cannot estimate has no box; untick anything it can estimate that the write-up should not carry. 3. Write the study period as it should read in a title: 1854. 4. Say what one row counts if it is not a person. An ecological study counts groups — sub-districts, wards, districts — and this is where that is said once instead of in every caption. 5. Connect it, or leave it upstream. Wiring it to an epi widget's design port states which declaration governs that computation. Where there is no edge, anything downstream of it finds it by walking back through the graph.

If you are not sure which design you have, leave it out. Everything computes as it did before, and a guessed declaration is worse than none.

What is asked after you select a design

Surveillance is not on the list. It says where data came from, and a study of any design can use such data. It is an answer to the source question below. A workflow that only describes surveillance counts declares no design.

For a cohort or an ecological study, the first page after the design is the table: you name the groups and the outcome and say what exposure is known for. The dialog draws the 2×2 in those words and marks the totals the study fixed. Select a cell to say what it counts and where it comes from, or that it was worked out from other cells. There are no numbers on this page: they come with the data, so it works for a study not yet begun. The other designs do not have this page yet.

The dialog runs one page at a time with Next, Back and Close. There is no Save: every change is kept as you make it. Selecting a design sets its questions. Where the table already says where each cell comes from, the first asks only whether any of it comes from a surveillance system. A blank for the group is filled from the table page, and you can change it. For a case-control study that means how cases arose, when controls were sampled, whether they were matched, and where they came from. Each answer writes a sentence into Methods, and some carry a caveat. Answer *not sure / not stated* when that is the truth: nothing stops, and the note says what is unknown. A blank you leave stays visible in the sentence as ‹blank›.

Answers stay stored if you change design, so trying another one loses nothing. Three questions come with every design: who or what decided who was exposed, how time is structured, and whether the outcome can spread or cluster. If exposure was decided outside the investigators, two more follow: what supports that claim, and whether to call this a natural experiment. That term has more than one definition, so the note always names which one it means, and it never licenses causal language. The wording of these questions is untested.

The checklist

The last page of the dialog reads your workflow against your design, and the Inspector gives the counts.

Read from this workflow is checked against the canvas and changes as you build: whether a two-by-two reads the design, whether data are connected, whether each input says where it came from, whether the result reaches an output. It says the workflow holds these things, not that they are right.

Declared by you is what you stated. Fieldwork records it and cannot check it.

The checklist reports and does not grade. Nothing on it stops a run. *Open* means no answer yet, and *stated as unknown* means you answered that you do not know, which is a different fact. *Differs* means your words and the computation's do not match: they may still be one group, and that is for you to judge.

What it will not do

  • It will not work out your design from your data. Four counts look identical whether they

came from a cohort, a case-control study or a survey. Only you know which you ran.

  • It will not choose between two declarations. A computation has one design port, and it

takes one connection. Connect each design to its own computation: a workflow may hold two, on separate branches.

  • It will not declare a study whose investigators allocated exposure. The five designs are

observational, so answering that investigators allocated exposure stops the declaration, and computations run under neutral names.

  • It will not check that your period is consistent with your data. The period is text for a

reader and a title. Whether a denominator covers the numerator's period is not checked.

  • It will not travel to another workflow. A design governs the workflow it is in. A project of

six workflows may have six different designs, or none.

What it does not do yet

It governs the two-by-two only. A connected design decides what two_by_two reports: case-control keeps the odds ratio and drops the word risk, cross-sectional reports prevalence measures, and a case series reports no comparison measure. rate_ratio carries the design and is not changed by it.

An undeclared design is reported, not punished. With no design connected, every measure is still computed, under a name for its arithmetic: ratio of row proportions, cross-product ratio, difference of row proportions. A line says no design is connected. The numbers are the same as before; only the names differ, because a/(a+b) is a risk only under some designs. A practitioner with their own data may not be sure which design they have, and an application that refused to compute until told would be worse than one that stays quiet.

It does not make a result correct. It makes a wrong measure refusable. Whether the groups are comparable, and whether a denominator's period covers its numerator's, are untouched — and the period check rate performs today is string equality where the condition is coverage.

See [experiment 154](../experiments/154-a-workflow-declares-how-as-well-as-where.md) for the admission review, and [the study-design audit](../audits/study-designs-and-our-computations.md) for how the designs were chosen.

More than one exposure

Most investigations of a shared meal compare a whole menu. How were the exposures chosen? records whether they were named in advance or all compared as a screen. A screen raises a question and needs other evidence to answer it. With several exposures, describe the table's groups in general, such as *ate* and *did not eat*, because the same description applies to each. The checklist then says how many were compared, and does not compare each with the declared groups.
two_by_two:
Two-by-two table

The analysis under the table. It takes four counts — two groups by two outcomes — and reports the risk in each group, the risk ratio, the odds ratio and the risk difference, each naming the method that produced it. Read as events and units at risk instead, it reports the rate ratio.

What it does

A two-by-two is the central table of field epidemiology, and this application could draw one for months before it could analyse one: it showed the four counts and their margins and stopped there.

On Snow's South London people, built inside the application from two of his tables:

diedsurvived
Southwark and Vauxhall only844166,810167,654

Why this exists, and the number to be careful about

The same project carries a rate ratio of 8.40 on Snow's houses. The risk ratio here, on his people, is 5.35. Both are correct and they are 57% apart.

It is tempting to say that is because one is a rate ratio and the other a risk ratio. It is not. A risk ratio over the same houses is 8.401853429780243 — the rate ratio's value exactly, bit for bit. Deaths per house *is* a risk when a house can hold at most one death, so the two are the same division. Only the intervals differ, and only in the second decimal: 6.84 to 10.32 from the rate ratio against 6.85 to 10.31 here.

So what moves the number from 8.40 to 5.35 is the subject being counted: a house, or a person. And that is the one thing the familiar layout does not show. A reader who takes 8.40 for the risk ratio beside the houses table is right — and is thereby taught that the substitution is always safe, which it is not. Make the outcome common instead of rare and the two part company.

This widget supplies the estimate. Reading the denominator is still yours.

The names above assume a declared cohort. Connect a *Study design* and it decides what is reported. With none connected, every measure is still computed, named by its arithmetic:

With a cohort declaredWith no design connected
Risk ratioRatio of row proportions
Odds ratioCross-product ratio
Risk differenceDifference of row proportions

The numbers do not change. A line under the estimates says no design is connected, and the receipt records it, because *"risk ratio"* over an undeclared table claims a design nobody chose.

What you connect

records — a table holding one row per combination of the exposure and the outcome. Total it first with *Total within groups*: a cell matching more than one row is refused rather than added up here, because summing silently is how a two-by-two acquires subjects nobody counted.

Or a line list. Tick Each row is one subject and connect it directly: a cell is how many rows agree. The tick is yours to make, because a table does not say which it is, and the two disagree about an empty cell. In a table of totals a missing row means nobody counted it, and it is refused. In a line list everybody is present, so a combination nobody fell into is a true zero.

This cannot tell whether a person appears on two rows.

Several exposures. With a line list, tick more than one under Exposures to compare, and the result is one table with a row per exposure: the counts, the risk in each group, the ratio and its interval, and how many rows are left out, in neither group, whether nobody recorded the answer or the mapping did not name it. Oswego's 14 foods take one node. Under a declared case-control design the table shows the four cells and the odds ratio, and no attack rate, because the study fixed the columns. Choose a control group by choosing the non-case value; the others are named as left out.

The rows stay in the order you ticked them. Nothing is ranked or highlighted: seeing which exposure stands apart is the reading. The result says how many comparisons were made and that no interval is adjusted for that number. Exposures also overlap, so one food's association can belong to another, and this table cannot separate them.

Which columns are offered. The widget does not know which columns are exposures: you tick them. It leaves out the outcome, any column with more than 12 distinct values, and any column with a different value on every row, so a numbered ID is not offered. Once Exposed and Unexposed are chosen, a column must hold both, whether they are Y and N or 1 and 0. A column coded differently from those two is not offered, so recode it first.

Events and units at risk: the rate ratio. Under The outcome column holds, choose events and units at risk, then name the value holding the events and the one holding the units at risk. Each group then needs two rows, not two outcomes: Snow's Table IX gives deaths and houses per company.

Rate ratio 8.40, 6.84 to 10.32, log-normal. A unit at risk is not a non-case: a house can hold more than one death, and person-time counts nobody, so this layout has no $b$ and $d$ and no risk ratio. Units at risk may be person-time and need not be whole numbers; events must be. A group with no events keeps its counts and says why there is no ratio. The interval treats events as independent, which a transmitted disease is not, so it is narrower than clustered events warrant.

A declared study design decides whether a rate ratio may be reported: a cohort or an ecological study, the same designs that license one from a Poisson regression. Under any other design the step stops and says why. With no design connected the rate ratio keeps its name, because events over units at risk is a rate under any design.

This replaced the Rate ratio with an interval widget on 2026-11-05. That widget read only a Rate step's result; this reads the table. The numbers are the same to the last digit.

What it writes into the notes. A Methods note gives the four cells, each formula the declared design reports, the numbers substituted and the interval method, and cites the method. With several exposures on one node the formulas are written once, in symbols. The numbers are in the step's table, which a Table output connected to it draws in the write-up with a note of its own.

How to use it

Exposed / Unexposedwhich two of its values are being compared

The outcome column holdscases and non-cases, or events and units at risk

Why you name the two groups

Because a table may hold more than two. Snow's people-denominated table has three supply categories: 16 of his 32 sub-districts were supplied by *both* companies. That stratum is not an exposure group, and it is the reason Snow's sub-district comparison could not settle the question and he went to the house level.

Whatever you leave out is named on the result, and the totals are of the two groups you chose rather than of the table. A stratum silently excluded is the commonest way a two-by-two misleads.

Reading what you get

The four cells as a table, with the estimates carried on it, and a receipt holding each estimate's value, bounds, level and method by name.

Each estimate also carries the label the familiar layout prints for the same quantity, so you can find the row you were trained to look for:

this widget computesprinted as
risk ratio · Katz logRisk Ratio (RR)
odds ratio · Wald logOdds Ratio (cross product)
risk difference · Wald unpooledRisk Difference (RD%)

Read from Epi Info AI's results panel, not from Epi Info. That is a sibling project whose epi kernel was synthesized from the original, so these are a good deduction and not a verification — and every estimate records which, in epiInfoLabelSource. The receipt says deduced. If somebody reads the labels off Epi Info itself the source becomes verified, and the words may or may not change; that is a different claim and the field keeps the two apart.

Odds Ratio (cross product) keeps its qualifier on purpose: the same panel prints an Odds Ratio (conditional MLE) beside it, which is a different estimator and is not computed here. Dropping the qualifier would make this label claim both.

One scale difference, stated rather than reconciled. That panel prints the risk difference as a *percentage*. Snow's figure is 0.004093 here and 0.4093% there — the same quantity on a different scale, and the estimate says so where the number is, so nobody reads the two screens side by side and concludes the implementations disagree.

The equation, as a note for your Methods section

Every run machines a note into Methods on the Notes tab, writing the four cells as a, b, c and d — the letters every textbook formula is in, and the ones an FETP trainee is taught — and then each measure twice: once as the formula, once with this run's numbers substituted.

$$\mathrm{RR} = \frac{a/(a+b)}{c/(c+d)} \qquad \mathrm{OR} = \frac{ad}{bc}$$

Why both forms. A formula on its own restates a textbook. The same formula with your numbers in it lets a reader check the arithmetic without rerunning anything, which is the thing a Methods section is for.

Each interval method is cited, or it says no source has been read for it. A citation here is read off a source or it is absent; none is written from memory, because a plausible-looking reference is the kind of error a reader stops checking at.

methodsource
risk ratio · Katz logKatz D, Baptista J, Azen SP, Pike MC. Obtaining confidence intervals for the risk ratio in cohort studies. Biometrics. 1978;34(3):469-474. doi:10.2307/2530610
odds ratio · Wald logWoolf B. On estimating the relation between blood group and disease. Annals of Human Genetics. 1955;19(4):251-253. doi:10.1111/j.1469-1809.1955.tb01348.x

The note is editable like any machined note: editing it forks it into a note of your own, and the machined one goes on being rewritten by every run.

What it will not do

  • It will not claim agreement with Epi Info. These are standard methods, named honestly, with

labels deduced from a project built from Epi Info. A parity claim needs a parity suite nobody has written.

  • It will not treat an empty cell as a zero. An empty cell is unknown, and a two-by-two

computed as though it were zero would understate that group.

  • It will not add half a case to make a ratio computable. A group with no cases has no risk

ratio, and this says so. The usual repair is an assumption, not a measurement.

  • It will not withhold the estimates it can still compute. A zero cell removes the odds ratio

and leaves the risk difference perfectly well defined, so each estimate reports its own availability and its own reason.

  • It will not accept a table of rates or percentages. These estimates count subjects. A

non-whole number is refused, except as units at risk in the rate layout, which may be person-time.

  • It will not adjust for anything. This is a contrast between two groups as they were supplied.

The stratum you left out is excluded, not controlled for, and no estimate here is an effect.

  • It will not test a hypothesis. Chi-square, Mantel-Haenszel, Yates, Fisher exact and mid-P are

not built. They are a larger piece and were not started to meet a date.

  • It will not check that the equation it prints is the one the source paper states. The

formulas in the note were read off this widget's own code, so they state what it computes. That the code matches Katz and Woolf is a different question, and the computations audit that would answer it is not written.

Where it is used

The South London example: *Died or survived, by water supply*, and, in the rate layout, *Deaths per house, by water company*.
regression:
Regression

A model. Logistic regression for a case-control or cross-sectional study, reporting odds ratios; Poisson regression for counts over time or area, reporting rate ratios. Each estimate is adjusted for the variables you add.

What it does

The two-by-two gives crude measures. A published study usually reports adjusted ones: the Salmonella outbreak's Galia melon odds ratio adjusted for age group and sex, NYC's ozone rate ratio adjusted for the other pollutants, temperature, holidays and time. This fits those models in Fieldwork's own kernel, by iteratively reweighted least squares, and builds the model's columns as R does, so the same model here and in R has the same columns and the same estimates.

What you connect

records — a table. The outcome and every variable are its columns: its key columns and its value column alike. design — optional, the study design. A declared design decides what the result may be called, and which model it allows.

It gives back a table: one row per reported term, with the ratio, the interval limits and p (with several exposure columns, one row per model and term; see below). The table says which statistic is the ratio and which are its limits, so Chart draws each ratio with its interval without guessing from the names.

How to use it

ExposureThe column whose ratio you want, as numeric (a ratio per unit), categorical (a ratio per value against a reference value) or a spline

Municipality, year and month together compare each week only with weeks of the same municipality, month and year. Absorbed, so thousands of strata cost little
