A row missing any variable the model uses is left out, as R does by default, and the result says how many and why.

One model per exposure column

Under Exposure, Also fit, one model each, with lists the table's other columns. Tick one or more, and the step fits one model per column: the same model each time, with only the exposure swapped. This is for a lag-response question, where Relate a column from another table has brought the temperature at several shifts, one column each.

  • Each model is fitted on its own rows. A week with no value at one shift is left out of that shift's model only.

Fitting every model on the weeks that have a value at every shift would be a different analysis, and is not done.

  • The models come out as one table, one row per model, term and statistic. Its columns are exposure (the

column the model is for), shift_days (the shift Relate recorded, as a number of days; only when there is one), role (*exposure* or *adjusted for*), term and statistic. To chart one point per lag, keep the rows whose role is *exposure* with Select rows by value, and choose shift_days as the chart's category column.

  • A column that cannot be fitted is a row saying so, with empty values, and the result says why. The step stops

only when no column can be fitted.

  • The result says how many intervals there are, and that none is adjusted for the number of comparisons.

An adjusted variable can follow the shift. With several models, each adjusted variable has a box, *follows the shift: each model is adjusted for its own column*. Tick it, and a column is chosen for each model, filled in Relate's order and each one changeable. The 2010–2025 Brazil workflow uses it: the model of the temperature 2 weeks before is adjusted for the rainfall 2 weeks before, from a second Relate that brings the rain at the same lags. The result says *each adjusted for precip_total_semana at its own shift*.

Untick every column to go back to one model.

What it will not do

It will not choose the variables. It fits what it is given; deciding what to adjust for is the investigator's.

It will not report a model that did not converge, or one whose columns carry the same information twice (collinear). It says which.

A declared study design decides the measure, read from the same declaration the Two-by-two table reads:

With no design connected the measure keeps its plain name, odds ratio or rate ratio, and the receipt says no design was declared. The NYC study, a time series of daily counts, is none of these five and is run without one. Experiment 176.

It does not do model selection, interaction terms, random effects, conditional logistic regression for individually matched studies, or exact methods.

find_satellite_products:
Find satellite products

Which satellites and products measure a variable, and what each one measures. It chooses where satellite data will come from. It downloads nothing.

What it does

Type a research topic or a measurement, such as *NO2 air pollution in New York City*, or pick a topic. The dialog shows the chain from the question to a provider's collection, a caution about what a satellite measures, and one card per product:

On each cardWhy it is there
Sign-inNo sign-in, no account (an anonymous token), or needs an account. Products needing none come first
MeasuresA column through the atmosphere, an optical depth, an index, or a near-surface value
UnitAs read from the product's own file, or "read from the file when it is opened"
LicenceAs read from the licence itself, with the date it was read; or "not yet read"
CitationThe dataset citation the producer asks for, with its DOI, the files it covers and the date it was read; or "not yet read"
In a browserWhether a browser has been shown to read it, and how that was checked
QualityThe product's own quality rule, where it has been read

Choose a product and the Inspector summarises it. Its output is a satellite product, which only a catalog search can take.

How to use it

1. Add Find satellite products from Sources. It needs no input. 2. In the Inspector, press Find satellite products…. 3. Type a topic or a measurement, or press a topic. Read the caution, then the cards: open products are first. 4. Press Choose this product on the one you want, then Done. The Inspector shows your choice. 5. Run the workflow: the run records which product was chosen and what was and was not read about it, in the N3 & evidence view.

Why it matters which quantity a product measures

A ground monitor measures air at the surface. A satellite NO₂ product measures the NO₂ in a column of air from the ground to the top of the troposphere; an aerosol optical depth measures how much the whole column dims light; most ozone products measure the whole atmosphere, mostly the stratosphere. They can move together with the monitors over time. They do not agree in value, and a card never lets them look as if they should.

Why the licence is read, not taken from the catalog

Planetary Computer gives Sentinel-5P's licence as *proprietary* and links an address that no longer exists. The licence itself, read at its new address, grants free, full and open access with attribution. So a card states the licence as read, where and when, and says when nobody has read it.

Where the products come from

The topics and most routes are JLT's, from the EO Satellite Guide (MIT), vendored unchanged at commit 684833c. Fieldwork adds the routes that need no sign-in, an ozone topic, and the facts on each card, read in [experiment 179](../experiments/179-eo-and-stac-for-the-nyc-monitors.md).

What it will not do

  • It will not download anything, or say that a product has data for your place and dates. That is the catalog

search's question.

  • It will not cite a product nobody has read a citation for. The three Sentinel-5P products on Planetary Computer

carry ESA's citations, read from the TROPOMI product pages on 2026-11-06. ESA gives one DOI per processor version, and these are Version 02, for the processor 2.x files Planetary Computer serves for June 2023. Every other card says "not yet read".

  • It will not choose for you. The order puts open products first; which one suits a study is yours to decide.
  • It covers what has been curated. A topic with no curated product says so rather than guessing one.

Where it is used

The NYC example, *Did the satellite see the city's NO₂?* (1 to 14 June 2023).

03 · Inspect & reuseThe selected item's files, with sign-in, the licence as read, whether a browser can read it, and the attribution sentence to use, and the dataset citation with its DOI where it has been read

How to use it

1. Add Find satellite products and choose a product. 2. Add Search a satellite catalog, and connect the product to product. If the workflow has a Study area, connect it to area and its extent is searched. 3. In the Inspector, press Search the catalog…. With no Study area connected, type West, South, East and North; the dialog says what is wrong with an edge until all four make an extent. Choose From and Until, and press Search. 4. Select an item, on the map or in the list, to inspect its files. Untick any item you do not want to keep. 5. Press Done, then run the workflow. The run records the search and how many items were returned, matched and kept.

What a search can and cannot tell you

A search tells you whether there was an overpass: which dates have an item over your area. It cannot tell you whether that overpass holds a usable value over your area. Clouds remove retrievals, and a product's quality flags mark others as unreliable. On 7 June 2023, the one Sentinel-5P NO₂ overpass of New York City came as two items, and the near-real-time one measured had no pixel passing the usual quality threshold. So every item says its completeness is not known until a reader opens the file, and the run records that it was not read. Sample satellite files at points is the reader.

One overpass can be two items

A Sentinel-5P orbit is published in more than one processing stream: near real time (NRTI, within hours, in five-minute pieces) and offline (OFFL, days later, the whole orbit, with better inputs). Each is an item, so one overpass can appear twice. Each item says its stream and orbit. Where an orbit has an offline item, its near-real-time items are not kept by default, so a reading is never counted twice; the product recommends the offline stream for time series. Tick one back if you need it.

What it will not do

  • It will not download a file. Reading the pixels at your points is a separate step, not yet built.
  • It does not stop at a number of items. Sixteen years of MODIS over Rio de Janeiro state is 2,891 items, read in

29 pages in about 19 s. Up to 0.40.0 it stopped at 500, the bound of the STAC Browser it was adapted from.

  • It keeps only the files a reader reads. A MODIS item lists 15 files and the reader uses 6, so the other 9 are

not stored; the search says which were kept and how many each item offered. A product with no reader keeps them all.

  • It will not search all time. It needs dates.
  • It will not search across the antimeridian or by the outline of the area: the area's extent is searched, so

items over nearby water or another country can appear. West must be less than east; split an area across the antimeridian into two searches.

  • It will not cite a product nobody has read a citation for. It shows the citation Find satellite products

carries, and says "not yet read" otherwise.

Where it comes from

The search, its messages, its 500-item bound and the typed W/S/E/N extent are adapted from JLT's STAC Browser (MIT, commit 945d8b3), in Fieldwork's dialog style. [Experiment 179](../experiments/179-eo-and-stac-for-the-nyc-monitors.md) records why each file says what it says.

Where it is used

The NYC example, *Did the satellite see the city's NO₂?* (1 to 14 June 2023).

Sample satellite files at points or over areas

The satellite value at each of your points, or over each of your areas, for every overpass or period, read from the files Search a satellite catalog found. Each value comes with its quality. Where a point has no usable value, it says which kind of gap it is. Nothing is filled.

What it does

For each point and each file the search kept, it reads the value of the pixel whose centre is nearest the point. It fetches only the parts of each file it needs, by HTTP range, in the browser. The result is a long table: one row per point per overpass, plus one row per point for each day with no overpass.

ColumnWhat it holds
point_id, pointThe point, as the point layer names it. Where Point data read its ids from a table column, the id column takes that column's name, site for the NYC monitors, so the result relates back to the source on it
date, overpass_timeThe day, and the time the pixel was scanned
stream, orbitThe processing stream (OFFL offline, NRTI near real time) and the orbit
scanline, ground_pixelWhich pixel of the swath was read
the variable, e.g. nitrogendioxide_tropospheric_columnThe value, only where it passed the quality rule, in the unit the file states (mol m-2)
value_as_readThe value read, whether or not it passed
qa_valueThe pixel's quality value, 0 to 1
passes_qualityyes or no
gapWhere there is no usable value: no overpass, no retrieval or below quality threshold

Over areas

Connect a polygon layer to areas instead of points: municipalities from Join a table to the study area, or a Polygon layer. Or connect a Study area to area: its units, such as municipalities picked from an administrative boundary, are read as they are. One kind of place per node. This works for gridded products, which today means MODIS land surface temperature (8-day, 1 km). Sentinel-5P is still read at points only.

Each area is read by the cells whose centre is inside it, the rule Clip raster uses. A municipality made of several parts, such as one with islands, is one area. Where an area spans two of MODIS's tiles, both are read and added before the mean is taken.

ColumnWhat it holds
the place columnthe area's name; call it as the table you will relate it to does, such as municipio
period_start, period_endthe 8-day period the file covers
platformterra (mid-morning pass) or aqua (early afternoon), never pooled
layerdaytime or night-time
cells, cells_with_value, cells_passinghow many cells the area holds, how many had a value, and how many passed the quality rule: the mean rests on the last
value_min, value_maxthe range of the passing cells, in the unit chosen
clear_dayshow many of the 8 days were clear, on average, behind the passing cells
LST_Day_1km or LST_Night_1kmthe mean of the passing cells, in the unit chosen
gapno cell in the area, no retrieval or below quality threshold

The unit. The files state kelvin. Report temperature in offers degrees Celsius (K − 273.15), the default, degrees Fahrenheit (K × 9/5 − 459.67) or kelvin. The conversions are exact, and the result says which was applied. How the unit is known: each file states it, with its scale factor, in its own tags, and every file opened is checked. A file that states another unit stops the run and is named.

The quality rule for MODIS. Its documents explain its quality bits and recommend no rule. The default keeps cells the product made, of good or other quality, whose average temperature error is 2 K or less. *Good quality only* and *everything produced* are the alternatives.

Read the counts. Over Rio de Janeiro in February 2024 each 8-day value rested on about two clear days, and one week's value for Rio de Janeiro city came from 26 of its 1,400 cells. A mean is reported wherever any cell passed; whether that is enough is the analyst's call, and the numbers to make it are on the row.

How to use it

1. Build the search first: Find satellite products (choose the Sentinel-5P NO₂ product on Planetary Computer), then Search a satellite catalog over your area and dates, and press Search. 2. Add Sample satellite files at points. Connect your point layer, for example the monitors from Point data, to points, and the search to files. 3. In the Inspector, check the Quality rule. It is set to the product manual's: qa_value at or above 0.75. 4. Connect a Table output, and run the workflow. The files are read during the run, and each file is read once per session. A year of files takes minutes: while they are read, a panel at the foot of the page names the step and counts the files read so far, *Reading satellite files: 40 of 92*, and the run's state beside the canvas says the same.

Several files are read at once: six MODIS files, three Sentinel-5P. Three months of MODIS over Rio de Janeiro's 92 municipalities took 70 s one file at a time in Chromium and 23 s this way. A browser opens at most six connections to the MODIS server, so more would not help. A file that fails is tried three times; if it still fails, the run stops and names it. Each file is read once per session, so running again after a change downstream does not read it twice.

The three gaps

GapWhat happened
no overpassNo file kept for that day, or the point is outside the file's swath
no retrievalThe satellite passed over, and no value was retrieved at that pixel: usually cloud
below quality thresholdA value was retrieved, and the product's own rule says not to use it

They are kept apart because they mean different things for a study: cloud is not random, and a day the satellite missed is not a day it saw and rejected.

The quality rule

The NO₂ product's documents disagree, and only at exactly 0.75: the readme says *above* 0.75, the product user manual's table *at or above*. The Inspector lets you choose, and the result and its receipt say which was applied.

qa_value is stored as an integer from 0 to 100 and a scale factor of 0.01, so the rule compares the integers. The scale factor is stored as 0.0099999998, so a value stored as 75 multiplies out to 0.74999998, which would wrongly fail "at or above 0.75".

What it will not do

  • It will not fill a gap. Imputation is a separate, declared step (experiment 179, provisional statement 2).
  • It will not interpolate. The value is the nearest pixel's, on pixels of about 3.5 × 5.5 km at the centre of the

swath and wider at its edges. A pixel is not the value at the point.

  • It will not turn a column into a concentration. NO₂ here is a tropospheric column, molecules in the air above the

pixel, not a surface concentration a monitor measures.

  • It will not read other products yet. Sentinel-5P NO₂ (at points) and MODIS land surface temperature (at points

or over areas), both on Planetary Computer, have readers. Ozone and aerosols say so when connected.

  • It will not weight by population or by how much of a cell lies in an area. A cell counts whole, or not.
  • It will not keep readings between sessions. A reload reads the files again.

What it costs

The cost is in chunks, not pixels. An offline NO₂ orbit file is about 600 MB and stores each variable in compressed chunks of 2,086 × 225 pixels, so the first pixel of a chunk costs the whole chunk: about 2 MB each for latitude, longitude and quality, and 3 MB for the value, measured on 7 June 2023. Expect roughly 10–15 MB per overpass, much the same for 2 points as for 50 when they fall in one chunk. A month of daily overpasses is a few hundred MB.

How it was checked

The lab's check 35 reads a Sentinel-5P-shaped file with h5py, a different HDF5 reader, and recomputes every point's pixel by comparing every centre in the swath, then rebuilds the table row by row for both quality rules. It agrees. Against 0.2.0 it found a point near the edge of one of the file's chunks read from the pixel across the edge from the nearest one: fixed in 0.2.1. The file is synthetic, so this says nothing about a real orbit's content.

Where it comes from

Admitted, built and measured in [experiment 179](../experiments/179-eo-and-stac-for-the-nyc-monitors.md). The files are read with h5wasm 0.10.3, from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology, whose notice travels with Fieldwork in vendor/h5wasm-0.10.3-LICENSE.txt.

Where it is used

The NYC example, *Did the satellite see the city's NO₂?*: Sentinel-5P NO₂ at the four NO₂ monitors over 1 to 14 June 2023, related to their daily readings on site and date.

Notes

What it does

The Notes tab is the project's write-up. It shows every note from every workflow in the project, filed under the four parts of the body (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion), followed by References.

A note is one of four kinds:

  • quoted: an author's own sentence, carried verbatim.
  • derived: restated from what an input declares, such as its source.
  • machined: written by a widget about what it did; the next run rewrites it.
  • authored: written by you.

Each note has a function, which says what it does for a reader (context, rationale, source, method, verification, finding, limitation). An authored note can also answer two questions about its sources: whose words and whose argument.

How to use it

1. Choose Add note under the part of the write-up where the note belongs. 2. Write the note. The dialog shows questions to ask of that part; hide them once they are habit. 3. Choose its function. If it draws on literature, answer whose words and whose argument. 4. Add the works it cites under Citations. They are marked on the note and listed in References. 5. To show a picture with the note, open Image and choose a PNG, JPEG, WebP or SVG file. Write its alt text, what the picture shows for someone who cannot see it, and its caption, what a reader is to take from it. Both are required. 6. Choose Add note (or Save when editing) to keep it on the project.

A picture goes above the note's words, on the board and in the write-up. It is kept on this device by its digest, and an exported project carries it. A note whose picture is not on this device says so, with its caption.

A note can be moved to another part by dragging its card. Editing a machined note does not change it: the edit becomes an authored note that keeps the wording it was taken from.

The parts of the write-up

Each part has a job, and the questions under it are for checking a draft, not for structuring one. They are the same questions the Add note dialog shows for that part.

Introduction

Shows the gap in knowledge, why filling it matters, and what this study adds. Build it in two moves: the problem (background to the gap, why it matters, what earlier studies left open), then the purpose (the approach, what is new in it). Funnel from broad to narrow and end on the objective. About three paragraphs. It is not a history of the issue or a full literature review, and it holds no results.

  • What is the gap in knowledge, and why does filling it matter?
  • What did earlier studies leave open that this study addresses?
  • Does the last sentence state the objective?
  • Is anything here background a reader does not need, or a result?

Methods

Says exactly how the study was done, so someone could repeat it and judge it. Use subheadings, define every variable and how it was measured, describe original methods in detail and cite standard ones. A flow diagram can show how the rows or people studied were reached. Describe what was done, not what was found: a result belongs here only where it explains a choice of method, with the reason first.

  • Could someone repeat the study from what is written here?
  • Is every variable defined, with how it was measured?
  • Does every method have a result that answers it?
  • Is anything here a finding rather than what was done?

Results

States the findings that bear on the objective, without interpreting them. Mirror the Methods: every measurement described there has a finding here, in the same order. Let the tables and figures carry the numbers, and say in a sentence or two what each shows. Use the past tense.

  • Does each result answer a method, in the same order?
  • Is any sentence interpreting rather than reporting?
  • Does the text say in a sentence or two what each table or figure shows, without restating it?
  • Do the numbers add up, and agree with the tables?

Discussion

Interprets the results and justifies the interpretation, against what other studies found and the gap the study set out to fill. One plan is four paragraphs: the key result and the main conclusion; the results beside comparable studies; the major limitations, stated plainly; and recommendations for practice and for further study. It holds no new results.

  • Is each conclusion beside the result that supports it?
  • Does any conclusion or recommendation go further than the results support?
  • How do these results compare with similar studies?
  • Are the major limitations stated plainly, with what was done about them?

References

Assembled from what the notes cite: a source an input declares, a method a computation uses, and a work a note cites from its Citations tab. Cite a work from the note that relies on it.

These parts and their questions follow the CDC/TEPHINET scientific writing course for Field Epidemiology Training Program residents, in this application's own words.

Whose words, and whose argument

A note that draws on published work answers two questions. They are separate: a note can use a source's exact words and still be your argument, or be in your own words and only report.

Whose words? How much of the source's wording the note carries.

AnswerWhat it meansA reader checks it against
the source's exact wordsA quotation. Put it in quotation marks and cite the pageThe source, word for word
close to the source's wordingYour sentence still follows the source's words and order. Common while learning to paraphrase; revise it into your own words, or quote itThe passage, which it may copy more than it should
my words: one passageA paraphrase of one passageThat passage
my words: the main pointsA summary of one work or severalEach work it cites
not sureYou looked and could not tellA reviewer can help decide

Whose argument? Whether the note reports the works or argues from them.

AnswerWhat it meansA reader judges it by
what the works sayReporting what others foundWhether the works say it
what I make of themYour analysis, reasoning or synthesis, which may cite works in supportWhether the reasoning holds, and whether the works support it
not sureYou looked and could not tellA reviewer can help decide

Both are optional and read unstated until answered. A note on your own data, a step or a result draws on no literature and needs neither. When a note both reports and argues, consider writing two notes, one reporting and one with your reading, and linking them, so each can be checked on its own terms.

What each answer commits you to

  • Exact words: the passage itself, copied exactly. If the exact words do not matter, put it in your own.
  • One passage: read the passage in full. Watch for staying so close to its wording that it becomes "close to the source's wording".
  • The main points: read enough of each work to state its main point; an abstract can serve if the note says so. Watch for making works agree more than they do.
  • What I make of them: make the turn from the works to your reading visible (*which suggests*, *for this study, that means*). Watch for claiming more than the evidence allows, most of all causation from an association.

Examples

  • The source's exact words, from Snow, 1855: "no experiment could have been devised which would more thoroughly test the effect of water supply on the progress of cholera than this".
  • Close to the source's wording, the same passage: *No experiment could have been devised which would test the effect of the water supply on cholera more thoroughly than this one.* The wording and order are still Snow's.
  • My words: one passage, the same passage: *Because the two companies' customers did not differ in their houses or their surroundings, the arrangement circumstances had produced tested the water supply more thoroughly than any designed experiment could have.*
  • My words: one passage, from Murdock and colleagues, 2017, on their summer measurements: *In summer, the city's weather station read warmer than loggers in the vegetation where mosquitoes rest, by 3.0 to 4.2 °C in daily maximum.*
  • My words: the main points, of Mordecai and colleagues, 2017: *Transmission by* Aedes aegypti *peaks near 29 °C and stops below about 18 °C and above about 35 °C, with adult survival setting the upper limit.*
  • My words: the main points, of Murdock 2017 and Wimberly 2020: *Where temperature was logged at the places mosquitoes rest, it differed from the weather station's by enough to change modelled transmission, and the difference varied with season and land cover.*
  • What I make of them, from the Brazil example: *The leads match lag 0, so an association of that size arises without temperature causing cases, and lag 0 cannot be read as transmission.* It reports nothing a work says; it is a reading of this study's own results.

What it will not do

  • It does not check that a note is faithful to the works it cites, or that "my words" are. That is for the author and the reader; it seldom holds the source's text.
  • It does not quote for you. A sentence carried word for word from a source belongs in quotation marks, with its page.
  • The questions do not grade a note. A note that answers all of them can still be wrong.
  • It does not check that alt text describes the picture, or that you may publish it. The picture's source and terms

belong in the note or its citations.
